A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37·1°C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.
Laboratory investigations showed the patient's white blood cell count was 15·2 × 109 per L (normal 3·84–10·0), neutrophils 83%, C-reactive protein concentration (CRP)was 9·97 mg/dL (normal <0·5), procalcitonin concentration was 0·5 ng/mL (normal 0–0·5), and D-dimer concentration was 3490 ng/mL (normal 0–500).
A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules—raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces’ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16·76 × 109 per L, neutrophils 90·5%, CRP concentration 15·2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the pulmonary lesions and indicated that they were probably septic emboli (figure); arterial blood gas analysis indicated respiratory failure. Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and—according to culture antibiogram—ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states—specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli

input: A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds—entering a summer thunderstorm—where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of −25°C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 μg once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days—although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation—whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body—rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.
options: Primary Raynaud’s phenomenon, Frostbite, Bullous pemphigoid, Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis

A 49-year-old man with Wernicke's encephalopathy visited our hospital because of generalised weakness. He had lost more than 10 kg in weight in recent months and he reported dysphagia with a feeling of something being stuck in his throat. He also had symptoms caused by aspiration. He was referred to our dysphagia clinic for a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS). An initial visual inspection of the mouth showed a large cystic mass behind the tongue (figure). The lesion was also seen in the vallecula on a lateral fluoroscopic view (figure). Laryngoscopy and neck CT showed a giant cyst on the lingual surface of the epiglottis (figure). However, it was VFSS that unequivocally proved the cyst was the cause of the patient's dysphagia: the mass was seen to move through the upper oesophageal sphincter and enter the oesophagus itself, preventing the passage of food. It interfered with folding of the epiglottis, resulting in residue build up in the vallecula, and it caused aspiration during swallowing (video 1).We performed laryngeal microsurgery using a carbon dioxide laser to resect the 40 mm diameter cyst. The VFSS was repeated 4 days postoperatively and it showed almost normal oropharyngeal movement during swallowing (video 2). When the patient was discharged, he had no difficulty swallowing whatsoever and had begun to gain weight.
Epiglottic cysts are often found in adults. Most laryngeal cysts are asymptomatic and rarely large enough to cause symptoms. However, large laryngeal cysts may present with patients complaining of a sensation of having a foreign body in their throat, voice change, dysphagia, or dyspnoea. Surgical resection of large epiglottic cysts should be considered in patients with either dysphagia or dyspnoea. VFSS, also known as a modified barium swallowing examination, is considered the gold standard-method of investigating dysphagia. It allows for real-time observation of bolus flow in relation to structural movement throughout the whole of the upper aerodigestive tract.
options: Ultrasound, MRI of the neck, Videofluoroscopic swallowing study, Gastrofiberscopy

A 17-year-old competitive athlete was seen in our cardiology department 2 days after he experienced palpitations, dizziness, and syncope while swimming in a pool of salty-tasting water in Mallorca, Spain. He explained that after the palpitations he felt his subcutaneous implantable cardioverter defibrillator (S-ICD) deliver a shock. He then started swimming towards the side of the pool, but began to feel faint and passed out. After a few seconds, he regained consciousness and got out of the water. He was taken to a hospital in Mallorca and had no further problems apart from a painful, red area on his chest (figure), which disappeared within 1 day.He was fit and well when we saw him. The device was in its original position—on the left side of his chest in the mid-axillary line, at the level of T7—where it had been placed 2 months earlier for primary prevention because the patient had a diagnosis of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Examination of the electrogram (EGM) recorded during the episode showed a period of fast, sustained ventricular tachycardia that was treated with an internal shock, with a fixed energy level of 80 J at a low impedance of 24 Ω (figure). Further scrutiny of the EGM showed that the first shock was followed by 22 s of ventricular fibrillation. The S-ICD then delivered a further low impedance shock at 24 Ω with reverse polarity, which put the patient back into sinus rhythm (figure; appendix). When we tested the device in our hospital, we confirmed that it was working properly—ie, delivering shocks with a normal impedance of 57 Ω and a fixed energy level of 80 J.
2 months after the original incident, while skiing in the Swiss Alps, the patient experienced a further episode of dizziness that was later confirmed as caused by fast ventricular tachycardia. This time the device converted him back into sinus rhythm with a normal shock impedance of 64 Ω and an energy level of 80 J, without causing redness of his skin.
Our case raises possibly important issues about lithe, athletic patients with S-ICDs swimming in salty water. Indeed, we believe that part of the electrical current might have travelled from the subcutaneous lead, which is very close to the skin surface, through the salty water to the S-ICD generator, resulting in a reduced energy shock being delivered to the heart and explaining the erythematous lesion on his chest. The patient's physique—he was fit with very little subcutaneous fat—and the salinity of the water might have facilitated the short circuit. The first low impedance shock induced ventricular fibrillation, and the second converted him back to sinus rhythm.
Finally, it should be noted that movement of the subcutaneous device anteriorly may also result in a slight reduction in shock impedance—the effect of gravity and muscular movement while swimming prone tends to move the generator cranially and anteriorly. A 43-year-old man attended our hospital with a 2-day history of gradually worsening left-sided abdominal pain 6 months after he had a deceased-donor renal transplant—both native kidneys were left in place—because of end-stage kidney disease due to diabetes mellitus. The patient had a history of coronary artery disease and had previously had coronary artery bypass surgery; he was prescribed tacrolimus (2 mg twice a day), mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg twice a day), prednisolone (5 mg daily), carvedilol (25 mg twice a day), acetylsalicylate (81 mg daily), and fluconazole (200 mg daily); he smoked 20 packets of cigarettes per year—he quit 1 year before the kidney transplant and restarted 2 months after the transplant smoking ten cigarettes a day.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 145/90 mm Hg, heart rate was 96 beats per min and regular. We found left-sided abdominal tenderness with no rebound or guarding.
Laboratory investigations found a leucocytosis (12·8 × 109 per L; typical range 4·0–11·0), and elevated haemoglobin concentration (19·8 g/dL; typical range 14·0–18·0); haematocrit was 60% (typical range 41–50); serum creatinine concentration was 1.38 mg/dL (typical range 0·7–1·3).
x-rays of chest and abdomen were within normal limits. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and normal left ventricular systolic function, with an ejection fraction of 55% shown on an echocardiogram. CT angiogram of the abdomen showed complete occlusion of the left renal artery—by thrombosis and calcific atherosclerosis—and a non-vascularised atrophic left native kidney; the transplant kidney, in the pelvis, attached to healthy iliac vessels, was functioning well and had a good blood flow (figure). A hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of prothrombin G20210a and Factor V Leiden mutations, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2 glycoprotein Ib antibodies—found no causes indicating a prothrombotic state; genetic screening showed no JAK2 mutations.
The patient was diagnosed with left renal artery thrombosis due to post-transplant erythrocytosis. Aspirin, apixaban, and monthly phlebotomy were initiated with the aim to reduce the haemoglobin concentration to <17 g/dL. After a repeat negative hypercoagulable workup—including measurement of protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels, which were negative—at 6 months, the apixaban was stopped and the angiotensin-receptor blocker, losartan, was started and increased to optimum level. Additionally, the patient continued to have therapeutic phlebotomy to keep his haemoglobin concentration below 17 g/dL. The patient had continued to smoke tobacco after the transplant. We counselled him on the need to quit smoking, which he managed to do. At follow-up 2 years later, the patient had excellent kidney function, and he had not needed any phlebotomy in the previous 4 months.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis is common after kidney transplant occurring in about 10–15% of the transplanted population. Myeloproliferative disorders can present with erythrocytosis in the post-transplant patients and need to be excluded along with other malignancies—including breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma. Renal artery stenosis—present in our patient's left kidney due to calcification—and sleep apnoea may cause erythrocytosis. In patients with post-transplant erythrocytosis, a smoking history should be taken; screening for acquired cystic renal disease and renal cell cancer in native kidneys should also be done.
Post-transplant erythrocytosis can occur at any time between 8 months and 2 years after kidney transplantation; thromboembolic events—including cerebrovascular accidents, deep venous thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism—may occur; notably, native renal arterial thrombosis is unusual after a kidney transplant. Aspirin and angiotensin receptor blockade are the key strategies to manage post-transplant erythrocytosis; phlebotomy and theophylline may also be used.

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4·5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications—specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy—consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions—without any visible obstruction—and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum—as probably occurred in our patient—and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors—specifically infection with H pylori—aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.

A 32-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 3-week history of fever, cough, and general fatigue; he also reported a 1-month history of night sweats. The patient had no significant medical history; he had been previously fit and well and was prescribed no medications.
On examination he was generally unwell looking; his temperature was 38·8°C, his blood pressure 82/49 mm Hg, and he had a sinus tachycardia of 130 beats per min.
CT scans of the patient's chest and abdomen showed multiple pulmonary nodules and bilateral adrenal masses—in the left adrenal gland the lesion was 61 mm × 36 mm and in the right 90 mm × 63 mm (figure). 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an increase in tracer uptake in the multiple pulmonary nodules, the bilateral adrenal masses, and the thyroid gland (figure).Laboratory investigations showed hyponatremia (128 mEq/L; typical range 135–145), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase concentration (903 IU/L; typical range 124–222), soluble interleukin-2 receptor concentration (2140 U/mL; typical range 157–474), adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration (177 pg/mL; typical range 7·2–63·3), and low cortisol level (1·9 μg/dL; typical range 6·2–19). The plasma renin activity was markedly elevated at 16 ng/mL/h (typical range 0·3–2·9) with an aldosterone level at the lower end of the normal range (66·3 pg/mL; typical range 30–159).
Lung cancer markers—including pro-gastrin-releasing peptide, serum carcinoembryonic antigen, and cytokeratin fraction 21-1—were within normal limits. Cosyntropin stimulation testing demonstrated no response in plasma cortisol concentrations: at 0 min the concentration was 1·7 μg/dL; at 30 min it was 2·6 μg/dL; and at 60 min it was 1·8 μg/dL, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency.
Oral hydrocortisone improved the patient's general fatigue; his blood pressure returned to normal range and the hyponatremia resolved.
Histopathological examination of a sample of tissue obtained from a biopsy specimen of one of the adrenal masses showed lymphocytic infiltration with atypical and enlarged cells; immunohistochemical staining showed CD3 positive T-cell infiltration and CD20 positive B-cell infiltration. Epstein-Barr virus—using in situ hybridisation—was identified; CD20 positive B-cells showed Epstein-Barr virus positivity, indicating that B cells were infected with the virus. Additionally, Epstein-Barr virus was detected in a sample of blood using PCR: 2400 copies of Epstein-Barr virus DNA to 106 white blood cells (reference range <200 copies to 106). Considering the findings and the presentation in the round, we diagnosed grade 2 lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
Therapy with cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, oncovin, and prednisone—acronymed to CHOP—was initiated and then switched to rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, oncovin, cyclophosphamide, and hydroxydaunorubicin (R-EPOCH) therapy. However, invasion of the liver by lymphoproliferative tissue was detected, and the bilateral adrenal tumours had increased in size; the patient developed liver and renal failure and died 2 months after the diagnosis of lymphomatoid granulomatosis was made.
The differential diagnoses of pulmonary lesions with bilateral adrenal masses and adrenal insufficiency includes malignant lymphoma, granulomatous infections—tuberculosis and histoplasmosis—and lung cancer with adrenal metastases.
Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder driven by Epstein-Barr virus which occurs mainly in patients with no overt immune deficiency. Presenting complaints include fever, sweating, and weight loss; patients typically have pulmonary nodules, skin nodules, and other extranodal sites—including the CNS. The disease is challenging to diagnose and treat mainly because of its heterogeneous clinical presentations, rarity, and sparsity of data about treatment.
options: Malignant lymphoma, Granulomatous infectious diseases—including tuberculosis and histoplasmosis, Sarcoidosis, Lymphomatoid granulomatosis

A 31-year-old nulliparous woman attended our hospital for treatment of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. She had previously presented with vaginal bleeding and a 28 mm lesion had been found on clinical examination and shown on MRI. We aimed to adopt a fertility sparing strategy—neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by conservative surgery of the body of the uterus—since biopsy samples of both pelvic sentinel lymph nodes showed no signs of metastatic spread.The patient had no previous medical history of note.
She received three courses of a cisplatin and paclitaxel regimen. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography was carried out during the first cycle of chemotherapy because of moderate liver cytolysis; at that time, the uterine corpus was 48 mm and endometrial thickness 4 mm. MRI post-chemotherapy showed a partial tumour response, but most notably, there was a clear decrease in the size of the uterine body of nearly 20 mm—from 47 mm to 28 mm. The shrinkage began early after the third course of chemotherapy (figure).
A trachelectomy was then performed and the patient was allowed home after 3 days. She had no postoperative complications. At follow-up 36 months later, the uterus was measured at 27 mm on MRI.
Uterine atrophy has—as far as we are aware—not previously been described in patients undergoing chemotherapy; we have been unable to find a clear explanation for its aetiology in this case. However, on review of our patient's history, she said that for the few weeks before starting the treatment, she had adhered to a strict ketogenic diet—with no slow or fast sugars.
Recently, uterine atrophy and osteoporosis was reported in mice after food restriction by reducing an insulin-like growth factor. The uterine atrophy seen in our patient might therefore have been due to a radical change in the patient's diet combined with the chemotherapy regimen—although we appreciate this is highly speculative. Alternatively, the cisplatin, which has been reported to induce atrophy of striated skeletal muscle, may have been responsible—although a similar effect on smooth muscle has not been documented.
Fertility sparing management should be offered to a select group of young patients requiring treatment for early stage I cervical cancer located in the cervix, without evidence of extracervical metastasis, and of conventional histopathological types. In patients with tumours below 2 cm in size, surgery—in the form of a simple or radical trachelectomy, depending on local prognostic factors—are standard. In patients with tumours between 2 cm and 4 cm, two options should be considered: a radical trachelectomy using an abdominal approach or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by conservative surgery. The assessment of the oncological safety of both strategies is still currently unclear—although results of an exploration of the different options are pending; either way the aim is to obtain a uterine corpus of at least 40 mm so as to allow a potential at term pregnancy. Finally, removal of the uterus after childbearing is not necessary in patients that are diligently followed up (video).

A woman aged 66 years, with a history of nodal osteoarthritis, presented with cutaneous nodules on her fingers and flexion contractures. The patient was no longer able to make a fist or straighten her fingers completely (figure, A). Her second to fifth metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal, and distal interphalangeal joints were swollen and tender. There were several firm, red, raised, tender cutaneous nodules (figure, A, inset). The patient also had a firm, non-tender swelling over the extensor aspect of the right forearm (figure, B). There were no psoriatic skin or nail changes.Laboratory studies yielded normal results (complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, serum uric acid, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens).
Radiographs of the patient's hands showed soft tissue swelling, an erosion at the left ulnar styloid, and multiple intra-articular erosions at the proximal interphalangeal and distal interphalangeal joints bilaterally (figure, C). Radiographs of the patient's feet also showed multiple scattered peri-articular and intra-articular erosions at the proximal interphalangeal and distal interphalangeal joints (figure, D).
A biopsy from one of the cutaneous nodules located on the left second finger showed predominantly acellular dense dermal fibrosis with a loss of elastic fibres and the presence of myofibroblasts (figure, E–G).
The clinical and pathological findings of the patient were consistent with the diagnosis of fibroblastic rheumatism.
The patient responded to weekly methotrexate (10 mg). The skin nodules stopped growing, with no new lesions. The patient's joint pain improved, and her flexion contractures stabilised.
Fibroblastic rheumatism is a rare fibroproliferative disorder, characterised by the sudden onset of symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis associated with multiple, firm, tender, flesh-coloured to purplish cutaneous nodules (2–20 mm in size), typically on extensor surfaces of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and also over other peri-articular sites (eg, elbows, knees, ankles, and feet). Permanent flexion contractures of the fingers can develop rapidly. Laboratory investigations usually yield normal results. Radiography shows soft tissue swelling, which can progress to an erosive arthropathy. Histological findings vary from scar-like, fibromatosis-like, to relatively acellular (ie, morphea-like or nuchal fibroma-like) fibrosis.
Diagnosis of fibroblastic rheumatism is based on characteristic clinical findings in combination with histopathological findings. The differential diagnosis includes rheumatoid arthritis, gout, calcinosis, tendon xanthomas, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, and nodular scleroderma. Based on scarce available data, glucocorticoids or methotrexate, or both, are the most effective disease-modifying drugs.

A 40-year-old woman attended our hospital complaining of excessive darkening over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and the soles of her feet: she also said she got tired easily, had a burning sensation in her mouth, and had become increasingly forgetful over the past 12 months. Additionally, she reported having chest pain brought on by exertion for the past 2 months. She had no medical history suggesting malabsorption, recurrent epigastric pain suggesting a hookworm infestation, or blood loss. She said her diet was strictly vegetarian, as advised by the local Ayurvedic practitioner, and mainly comprised chapattis and dhal, with no fruit, milk, or vegetables. A physical examination confirmed deep brownish-black pigmentation over her fingers and toes, and on the palms of her hands, and soles of her feet (figure). Her scalp hair was brittle, her tongue was bald with brown pigmented spots, and she had brown pigmented spots all around the inside of her mouth. Examination of her cardiovascular system found a soft systolic murmur at the apex and a fourth heart sound. Neurological examination found diminished deep tendon reflexes with intact peripheral sensation. Romberg's sign was absent. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL, macrocytosis (mean corpuscular volume 107·9 fL), and white cell count 3·4 × 109 per L. A peripheral blood smear showed oval macrocytes, fragmented and teardrop shaped red blood cells, and hypersegmented neutrophils (figure). Serum folate concentration was 14·2 ng/mL (normal range 3–17), serum B12 concentration was less than 83 pg/mL (normal range 174–878), and serum homocysteine concentration was 34·69 μmol/L (normal range <15). A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed biphasic T waves in leads V1–V3. A coronary angiogram showed critical proximal stenosis in the left anterior descending coronary artery. The patient was treated with oral B12 supplements, statins, and antiplatelets, and advised to have a protein rich diet, with fruits and vegetables. 3 months later, her symptoms had greatly improved: the pigmentation of her skin was markedly reduced (figure) and her haemoglobin concentration had increased to 10·4 g/dL, with improvement in all red blood cell indices.Pigmentation of skin and nail beds is a sign of malnutrition often seen in patients with tropical sprue, strict vegetarians, and tropical megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. The mechanism underlying the hyperpigmentation is thought to be a decrease in glutathione levels—responsible for the activation of tyrosinase and the transfer of melanin to melanosomes. A defect in the melanin transfer between melanocytes and keratinocytes leads to hyperpigmentation.
Demonstration of macrocytes, abnormal shaped red blood cells—including teardrop shaped cells—and hypersegmented neutrophils is a cheap and easily available way of confirming vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia: the blood film remains an important, simple, and speedy investigation in outpatient departments in rural India.
options: Howell-Jolly bodies, Hypersegmented neutrophils, Schistocytes, Target cells

input: A 59-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and haemodialysis since 2008 was admitted with painful, non-healing ulcerations on his legs. The lesions developed without known trauma 2 months before admission (figure). Pedal pulses were palpable on both sides and there were no signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Radiography of the soft tissue revealed diffuse calcified arterioles in a mesh-like pattern (figure). Histological examination of skin biopsy showed sclerosis and thrombosis of blood vessels (figure) and von Kossa stains were positive for calcium deposits (figure), confirming the diagnosis of calciphylaxis.Calciphylaxis is a syndrome of systemic medial calcification of the arteries leading to tissue necrosis. Skin biopsy and radiographic features are helpful in the diagnosis; but negative results do not necessarily exclude the diagnosis. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, several comorbid conditions are known to increase its development. Associated risk factors in our patient were: end-stage renal disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon. Recent reports indicate that low parathyroid hormone levels in association with adynamic bone diseases can also be associated with calciphylaxis. Unfortunately, there is still no standardised treatment for calciphylaxis. Based on previous reports, phenprocoumon was withdrawn in our patient and he was treated with cinacalcet, daily haemodialysis, sodium thiosulfate, and bisphosphonate. After 4 weeks, skin condition improved and the patient was discharged home.
options: Peripheral arterial disease stage IV, Chronic venous insufficiency, Calciphylaxis, Pyoderma gangrenosum

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and weight loss.
4 months earlier, she had presented to the local district hospital because her work colleagues had thought she looked pale. The patient had been found to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 4·7 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear suggestive of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia. She had no other medical history. She was transfused 2 units of blood; she was investigated at the outpatient clinic but was not referred for endoscopic assessment.
On examination, we found the patient to be pale and cachectic. Her blood pressure was 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats per min, temperature was 37·0°C, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On palpation of her abdomen, we felt a discernible, non-tender right upper quadrant mass; she had no other abnormal findings.
Investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 565 × 109 per L (normal 150–400), and white cell count of 10·5 × 109 per L; the mean corpuscular volume was 77·2 fL (normal 80–94) and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin was 23·1 pg per cell—suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia. The patient's renal and liver function tests were unremarkable.
An abdominal CT scan showed—on axial view—a target-like lesion (figure) and—on coronal view—a sausage-shaped lesion at the third part of duodenum; the stomach appeared distended. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly elongated stomach with external compression at the second part of the duodenum.
We carried out an exploratory laparotomy and found a duodenojejunal intussusception. We were unable to manually reduce the lesion, and so carried out a segmental resection of third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with a side-to-side duodenojejunal anastomosis at the second part of the duodenum. Analysis of the excised lesion showed a 6 cm × 5 cm well-encapsulated and pedunculated tumour of the third part of the duodenum which acted as the intussusceptum telescoping into the proximal jejunum—the intussuscipiens (appendix). Histological analysis of samples of the tumour showed a poorly differentiated extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum. Immunohistochemistry stains demonstrated strong and diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity to NKX2-2 and ERG, with membranous immunoreactivity to CD99, and an absence of nuclear immunoreactivity to FLI1: supporting a possible fusion of the EWSRI gene on chromosome 22q12 with the gene encoding the transcription factor ERG (appendix). The tumour cells exhibited no immunoreactivity to cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, LCA, TdT, synaptophysin, chromogranin, desmin, myogenin, S100, and α-smooth muscle actin.
Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged after a week. One month later, she returned reporting persistent abdominal and lower back pain. An abdominal CT showed enlarged coeliac, para-caval, and para-aortic lymph nodes with no lung metastases in the lower half of the thorax. Skeletal x-rays of the axial and cortical bones displayed no osteolytic bone lesions. The patient was urgently transferred to the oncology clinic but died before treatment was commenced.
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the small intestine is an extremely rare tumour with poor prognosis. However, if detected early, it may be successfully treated with surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Young adults presenting with recurrent vomiting, weight loss, an abdominal mass, and anaemia should raise the suspicion of an aggressive malignancy (video).

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses—known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0·58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0·67), with a low FEV1 of 1·97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2·58 L), a normal FVC of 3·52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3·41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6·58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5·06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25·3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17·69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans—as our patient's imaging illustrates—may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices—including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica—may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

A 62-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension and well-controlled diabetes mellitus type 2 was found unresponsive on the floor at home by her family. Her family reported that the day before admission she had appeared more tired and weak with altered mental status, but before that had been in normal health. On examination she had Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 3, a temperature of 39·4°C, tachycardia, and systolic blood pressure ranging from 170–200 mm Hg. She had weakness in her legs bilaterally, but review of systems was otherwise negative. In view of her low GCS score she was intubated for airway protection, and required vasopressors because she was hypotensive, febrile, tachycardic, and not responding to fluids. A CT scan of her head and subsequent MRI showed profound hydrocephalus (figure).An external ventricular drain was fitted for possible acute hydrocephalus, but her intracranial pressure was found to be 5 mm Hg (normal 5–15 mm Hg) and remained 5–10 mm Hg so the drain was removed 2 days later. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests were normal. We made a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, on the basis of chest radiographs showing consolidation and blood culture results, as the cause of her altered mental status, which returned to normal after treatment with antibiotics. She was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and has now returned to her normal baseline. In view of her previously normal medical history the clinical team decided her hydrocephalus had probably been present since birth.
This case shows the brain's ability to maintain normal mental status and function in spite of profound chronic hydrocephalus. In contrast to normal pressure hydrocephalus, compensated hydrocephalus can be asymptomatic until an external insult, such as an infection as in this case, and can lead to syncope or even sudden death. Compensated hydrocephalus, also known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo, is a form of communicating hydrocephalus—ie, one that does not obstruct the flow of CSF. Compensated hydrocephalus is usually seen in elderly people as the result of brain volume loss due to ageing or a disorder that causes the brain to shrink, such as Alzheimer's disease, leukodystrophy, or encephalomalacia resulting from focal damage caused by a stroke or traumatic brain injury. Clinicians should be aware of this condition that might be found incidentally on imaging in asymptomatic patients. Unless dictated by clinical examination, as in this case, additional work-up is not necessary.
options: Cerebral aqueduct stenosis, Meningitis, Alzheimer's disease, Traumatic brain injury

A 71-year-old woman with a 3-month history of nausea, 5 kg weight loss, and a hypochromic microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·9 g/dL) was referred to our hospital by her family doctor for further investigation.On examination the patient was pale and had a palpable, non-tender epigastric mass.
Apart from the anaemia, laboratory investigations showed mild thrombocytosis (platelet count 589 × 109 per L) and elevated liver enzymes with a gamma glutamyl transferase concentration of 96 U/L and alkaline phosphatase concentration of 358 U/L.
Gastroscopy showed an ulcerating mucosal lesion on the lesser curve of the stomach which was biopsied and confirmed histologically as a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma; the tumour was human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) positive with an average HER2 gene copy number of 7·25 (normal <4·0), and an average chromosome 17 enumeration copy probe (CEP) number of 1·45 (normal <3·0), giving an elevated HER2: CEP17 ratio of 5·0 (a ratio of less than 2·0 indicates a negative result).
CT scan showed extensive epigastric, porta hepatis, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy with several hypodense liver lesions, consistent with multiple metastases (figure). The clinical diagnosis was stage 4: non-curable gastric carcinoma.
Following oncology assessment, the patient was deemed suitable for chemotherapy—accepting the target of the treatment was at best a short-term extension of a predicted median survival of approximately 12 months. Trastuzumab—a humanised IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds HER2-receptors in certain cancer cells inhibiting tumour cell growth—was prescribed in combination with cisplatin and capecitabine. She tolerated the chemotherapy well apart from some initial nausea; at follow-up 6 weeks after commencing treatment, she reported feeling well with no further nausea. At the 3-month review, the patient was clinically stable, and CT imaging showed that her cancer had resolved macroscopically; accordingly, cytotoxic chemotherapy was stopped at 18 weeks, but she continued trastuzumab therapy every 3 weeks for the next 7 years. At review, 21 months after stopping trastuzumab, the patient was still in complete remission, with no evidence on CT scan of malignant disease (figure).
In the Trastuzumab for Gastric Cancer (also known as ToGA) Trial, none of the HER2-positive randomly assigned patients with advanced gastric or oesophago-gastric cancer were alive at 36 months’ follow-up. However, as our case shows, some patients with HER2 receptor-positive gastric adenocarcinoma can experience complete long-term remission with good quality of life from protracted trastuzumab therapy.
options: Cisplatin, Trastuzumab, Capecitabine, Taxol

A 90-year-old woman was transferred to our hospital with a 7-day history of pain in the right upper quadrant of her abdomen, decreased appetite, and post-prandial vomiting. On examination, she was afebrile, mildly tachycardic, at 95 beats per min, and in atrial fibrillation. Her blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg. Clinically, she looked dehydrated and had a scar over the right hypochondrium, which was slightly tender, with a palpable mass, but she had no peritonism. In her medical history, she had a cholecystectomy approximately 50 years ago. She also had a history of breast cancer, atrial fibrillation, and pacemaker insertion.A CT scan of the abdomen showed pneumobilia and obstruction of the gastric outlet with severe gastric dilatation: a hyperdense, discrete lesion with lamellated markings, resembling a gallstone, was also seen in the immediate post-pyloric region (figure). We attempted to insert a nasogastric tube to relieve the gastric distention but failed despite several attempts. We therefore decided to take the patient to theatre to do a gastroscopy. We found an oesophageal diverticulum—which explained why we could not insert a nasogastric tube—and a large gallstone in the pylorus, which we could not retrieve with the gastroscope, so we did a laparotomy. We could not push the gallstone into the stomach, so we removed it by doing a Heineke-Mikulicz pyloroplasty. Biochemical analysis confirmed a cholesterol-rich stone mixed with calcium, measuring 50 mm×15 mm (figure). The patient made an uneventful recovery.
Bouveret's syndrome is an uncommon presentation of obstruction of the gastric outlet and a rare form of gallstone ileus; it is caused by a gallstone passing through a cholecystoduodenal fistula, impacting the duodenal cap, and causing secondary obstruction of the gastric outlet. Radiological investigation may show Rigler's triad: pneumobilia, obstruction, and ectopic gallstone.
This is the first case, to our knowledge, of a gallstone causing a gastric outlet obstruction in a patient who had previously had a cholecystectomy. It raises the question— how could a stone have moved via a fistula from the gallbladder to the stomach when the patient reportedly had no gallbladder? Two possibilities: first, the move occurred via the fistula before the cholecystectomy; second, if the patient had undergone a subtotal cholecystectomy, the stone may have formed later in the cystic remnant and caused a choledochoduodenal fistula that allowed the gallstone to pass into the stomach. Whatever the answer, Bouveret's syndrome—an uncommon cause of right upper quadrant pain—is associated with a high risk of morbidity and mortality and should be considered a differential diagnosis alongside more common causes like cholecystitis, pancreatitis, perforation of a peptic ulcer, or other causes of obstruction.

options: Duodenal malignancy, Bouveret’s syndrome, Gastric polyp, Peptic stricture

A 64-year-old man presented with high fever (38–39°C oral temperature), severe joint pains with explosive onset, and substantial weight loss (4 kg in 1 month). On examination, he had dorsal oedema on the hands (figure) and symmetrically tender and swollen joints (ie, proximal interphalangeal joints, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, and knees). Additionally, he had generalised lymphadenopathy (bilateral upper cervical, left lower cervical, right supraclavicular, bilateral inguinal) and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations were notable for anaemia (haemoglobin 8 g/dL), hypoalbuminaemia (2·8 g/dL), hyperglobulinaemia (5·2 g/dL), increased erythrocyte sedimentation (35 mm/h), and increased concentrations of C-reactive protein (11·3 mg/dL). Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide were negative. PET scanning with 18-fluorodeoxyglucose showed avid lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm and uptake in both shoulders and the right wrist (figure). A cervical lymph node was excised for haematoxylin and eosin staining that showed architectural effacement by lymphoid cells (positive for PD-1 and CD3) surrounding an arborising network of high endothelial venules, which was suggestive of angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (figure). The patient was transferred to the haematology unit where chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (known as the CHOP regimen) was initiated, which resolved the fever and arthritis.Many aetiologies can cause fever with polyarthritis: infections (viral infections, infective endocarditis, Lyme disease), para-infections (rheumatic fever, reactive arthritis), true arthritis (adult-onset Still's disease), connective-tissue diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus), vasculitis (giant-cell arteritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis), and paraneoplastic arthritis. Paraneoplastic arthritis is arthritis secondary to solid-organ (particularly carcinomas) or lympho-reticular malignancy, which is not due to direct tumour infiltration. Important clues for paraneoplastic arthritis include advanced age, explosive onset, severe pain disproportionate to the pathological findings on examination, unresponsiveness to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), substantial weight loss, highly increased acute-phase reactants, and seronegativity for rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibodies. Specific patterns such as asymmetric arthritis, lower-limb predominance, sparing of small joints, palmar fasciitis, and remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting oedema should alert the clinician to investigate for an underlying malignancy.
In this man's case, the underlying malignancy was angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Although an uncommon non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall (1–2% of all patients diagnosed with lymphoma globally), it is common in patients with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (18% prevalence) and typically occurs in older people (median age 65 years). Angio-immunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is notorious for immune-activation features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenia, polychondritis, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and even positive autoantibodies. These symptoms are thought to be secondary to increased serum concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines, notably TNFα and interleukin-6 secreted by the tumour cells. The case highlights the importance of clues such as disease onset at an older age, explosive-onset joint pain, weight loss, and a thorough general examination (to detect lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly) to make an accurate diagnosis of paraneoplastic arthritis.

options: Symmetric arthritis, Increase of acute phase reactants, Explosive-onset arthritis, Involvement of small joints

A 5-year-old girl presented to her primary care physician with swellings on both sides of her neck. She was referred directly to the Center for Oncology, in Minsk, because she had been living 70 miles away from the Chernobyl Power Plant at the time of the accident, in the Gomel District of Belarus. An ultrasound scan of the area showed a suspicious nodule of more than 2 cm in diameter in her thyroid gland as well as multiple bilaterally enlarged lymph nodes in the neck. She had a thyroidectomy and bilateral lymphadenectomy. Histology showed an invasive papillary thyroid cancer over 2 cm in diameter and bilateral lymph node metastases (pathological stage T4N1bM0). The girl was given levothyroxine postoperatively to prevent hypothyroidism and to suppress TSH. However, because of the low quality of the drug available at that time, TSH suppression was not permanent and 2 years later, tumour recurred in a lymph node on the right side of the girl's neck and was removed during a unilateral dissection. She was then given a course of radioiodine therapy (RIT). A scan done after treatment showed intense uptake of iodine-131 (131I) in both lungs; a chest x-ray was normal. The RIT was repeated three times at intervals of 4–6 months (cumulative activity 5·3 GBq of 131I). However, because no change occurred in the level of 131I uptake in the lungs, it was thought that the metastases were not responding to the RIT, and five courses of chemotherapy with bleomycin were given, again without any clear metastatic response.The patient's clinical course and the small amounts of poor-quality—selenium-75-contaminated—131I available in Belarus resulted in her being selected for treatment at the University of Essen, Germany, where she had her fifth course of 3 GBq of 131I, given in hypothyroidism—to ensure a high uptake of 131I—with a raised TSH concentration (>80 mU/L). The patient's parathormone and serum calcium concentrations were both low, leading us to treat her for postoperative hypoparathyroidism. A post-therapy scan showed intense 131I uptake in the lungs (figure) and a correspondingly high serum concentration of the thyroid-specific tumour marker thyroglobulin of 3750 ng/mL, which should be undetectable after thyroidectomy if all benign or malignant thyroid tissue is removed.
The RIT was repeated five more times and 131I uptake in the lung metastases finally disappeared (figure). At her last follow-up examination, in the Gomel District, in September, 2019, no scintigraphic or radiological remnants of pulmonary metastases were seen. The patient's thyroglobulin concentration had decreased considerably to 17 ng/mL (classed as a stable partial response), mild pulmonary fibrosis was seen on a lung CT, and pulmonary function was reduced. The patient trained as a kindergarten teacher. 1 year after marrying, she gave birth to a healthy son, in 2007 (figure). Both patient and son are doing well and living in the Gomel District.
Treating differentiated thyroid cancers in children with RIT has short and long term side-effects—including thyroiditis due to irradiation, gastritis, nausea, bone marrow suppression, secondary primary malignancies (leukaemia and solid tumours), and—as in our patient—pulmonary fibrosis.

A 63-year-old woman with a 3-day history of sudden, painless visual loss in her left eye primarily affecting the inferior part of her visual field, presented to our clinic. She reported no headache; no pain in the temple, jaw, or ear; no migratory arthralgias; or intermittent fevers.
The patient had a history of systemic hypertension and was prescribed lisinopril. On examination, she was afebrile; blood pressure was 164/85 mm Hg and pulse was 85 beats per min. Visual acuity was 6/12 with the right eye and 6/60 with the left eye; the visual field of the right eye was full; the left eye visual field had a dense inferior field defect (figure). The right pupil was normally reactive to light; the left pupil was sluggishly reactive, and there was a moderate left relative afferent pupillary defect.
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed mild cataracts in both eyes. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm bilaterally. On ophthalmoscopy, the right optic disc was slightly small and had no central cup (figure); the left optic disc was swollen and hyperaemic, associated with several peripapillary flame-shaped haemorrhages (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haematocrit of 41% (typical range 36–48 in women); erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 35 mm/h (normal value for age <37 mm/h), C-reactive protein concentration was 0·4 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L), and platelet count was 310 000 per mL.
A diagnosis of non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) was made and the patient was advised to see her internist for a complete physical examination; she was told that there was no consistently beneficial treatment for the condition but that some patients experienced spontaneous mild visual improvement. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's visual acuity and visual field were stable, and her left optic disc was now pale.
NAION is the most common cause of sudden, unilateral, optic nerve-related visual loss in patients over the age of 50—albeit, in rare circumstances, it can occur in those younger than 50. The condition is characterised by variable loss of visual acuity associated with a visual field defect that often affects the upper or lower field of vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a swollen, usually hyperaemic optic disc. Peripapillary flame-shaped haemorrhages are often seen. Men and women are equally affected, and most have one or more underlying systemic vascular disorders such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidaemia that may not be known at the time visual loss occurs.
The pathogenesis of NAION is unknown but an almost universal feature is that instead of there being a normal-sized central depression in the optic disc—the optic cup—in both the affected and the fellow eyes, the cup to disc ratio is relatively small compared with the general population; this anatomical abnormality is thought to predispose the optic disc to ischaemia—particularly in patients with one or more underlying systemic vascular disorders.
Physicians seeing an older patient with sudden, painless, unilateral visual loss and a swollen optic disc should differentiate NAION from arteritic AION—the most common cause of which is giant cell (also known as temporal) arteritis.
Patients should also be referred for a complete physical examination to determine whether there are any underlying systemic vascular disorders; control of such disorders may reduce the 15–20% 5-year risk of NAION in the fellow eye as well as reducing the risks of stroke, heart attack and death, all of which are increased in patients with NAION compared with age, sex, and vascular disorder-matched populations.
output: Most patients have underlying systemic vascular disease that may not be known at the time they loss vision
target: Prompt treatment with systemic corticosteroids will result in visual improvement in most patients
options: Most patients have underlying systemic vascular disease that may not be known at the time they loss vision, Patients with NAION in one eye have a 15-20% risk of developing a similar event in the fellow eye, Prompt treatment with systemic corticosteroids will result in visual improvement in most patients, Patients with NAION have an increased risk of stroke and heart attack

A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-week history of abdominal pain, jaundice, and pruritus.The patient had a history of gout; his alcohol consumption was 7 drinks per week, and he had a 10-pack-year smoking history which ended when he quit 8 months earlier. He had no history of recent travel or contact with any ill people.
On examination, he had scleral icterus, a soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses or organomegaly; he had no stigmata of chronic liver disease or palpable lymphadenopathy. He was afebrile with vital signs in normal range.
Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 7·1 × 109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration 123 g/L, creatinine concentration 82 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase of 510 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 825 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 298 U/L, and a total bilirubin of 169 μmol/L. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a mild polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The serum IgG4 concentration was mildly elevated at 2·05 g/L; the IgG1 was elevated at 11·9 g/L and IgG3 was elevated at 2·03g/L. Tumour markers were normal. Ferritin was raised at 707 μg/L, transferrin saturation was 12%. Hepatitis B, C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus serology were all negative. CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed marked intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct dilation; there were no intraluminal or adjacent extrinsic lesions, but the pancreas was diffusely enlarged, and there was bilateral renal enlargement with poorly enhancing nodules. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a distal common bile duct stricture (appendix), and histopathological examination of biopsy samples of the pancreas obtained by fine needle showed active and chronic inflammation; no IgG4-positive plasma cells or malignancy were identified. Our working diagnosis at that stage was an autoimmune pancreatitis and the patient was prescribed prednisone; initially his condition improved, and he showed a good response. However, six months later, he returned reporting fatigue and weight loss. Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 45 mg/L and creatinine concentration of 200 μmol/L.
A repeat CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed noticeable changes when compared with the earlier imaging, extensive lymphadenopathy, a bulky pancreatic head, hepatomegaly, and bilateral nephromegaly, were observed.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a cervical lymph node obtained after an excisional biopsy showed expansion of the sinuses by histiocytes (appendix), with lymphocytic emperipolesis (figure). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated the histiocytes were positive for CD68 and S100, and negative for CD1a. The clinical presentation and histological findings were consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. He was prescribed rituximab, which led to the complete resolution of his symptoms. At follow-up one year later, he remained in complete clinical, radiological, and biochemical remission.
Obstructive jaundice results from a disruption in the flow of bile due to complete or partial obstruction of the extrahepatic biliary system. Common causes in mid-life include choledocholithiasis, choledochal cysts, bile duct strictures secondary to chronic pancreatitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma. RDD is a rare histiocytic neoplasm that classically presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Pancreatic RDD can be mass-forming and may mimic malignancy, infection, or autoimmune pancreatitis—both non-IgG4-related and IgG4-related (video).
options: Pancreatic cancer, Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease, IgG4-related pancreatitis, Cholangiocarcinoma

Five children—whose ages ranged from 3 to 11 years—attended our temporary medical camp complaining of variously sized protrusions in their abdomens pushing the umbilicus forward. The lesions had been present in all the patients since birth. All the children were spontaneous, normal vaginal deliveries, but none had been assessed by a doctor within the past 12 months. Interestingly, the remote village of Pataase, where we located our camp to provide basic medical care, in a rural area 25 km north of Cape Coast, the capital city of the Central Region of Ghana, was home to a total of 75 children—including the five (figure) with the umbilical protrusions.The three older boys were aged 11 years, 8 years, and 5 years. The two younger boys, whose mother is pictured with them, were identical twins and 3 years old. On physical examination, the umbilical protrusions were all reducible and painless. The aetiological abdominal wall defect under the protruding umbilicus was easily felt, so we made a diagnosis of an umbilical hernia in all the children. We referred all five patients to the nearest hospital for further assessment.
Umbilical hernia is a common condition found in children. The incidence ranges from 10 to 25% of newborn babies, and it appears to be more common among African populations for reasons that are not well understood. The condition is also associated with babies that are either premature or of low birthweight. In utero, the umbilical cord passes through the umbilical ring—a defect in the linea alba—to reach the fetal circulation. After birth, the umbilical ring usually closes spontaneously, with closure occurring within the first 5 years of life, but it may take up until the child reaches teenage years. Without closure, the small intestine can herniate through the umbilical ring; the extent of the fascial opening of the umbilical ring—not the size of the herniation—determines the likelihood of spontaneous closure. Often, the umbilical hernia is reducible—as in our cases. The situation is most serious when the hernia is incarcerated and becomes irreducible: such patients will complain of tenderness and firmness, and erythema will be seen around the hernia. At this stage the umbilical hernia may become strangulated and even rupture.
Management of umbilical hernia begins with observation. If it is reducible and slowly decreasing in size, the recommendation is to watch and wait. Children with large umbilical hernias that do not appear to decrease within the first 2 years of life are candidates for surgical correction. Surgical intervention is certainly indicated in incarcerated umbilical hernia.
options: Hyperthyroidism, Mucopolysaccharidosis, Trisomy 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-day history of a fever and who had, for the past 4 days, an impaired level of consciousness attended our hospital.She had a medical history of autoimmune encephalitis and urinary tract infections.
On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38·11°C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14·20 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0); absolute neutrophil count was 13·83 × 109 per L (normal 1·8–7·5) with a percentage of 97·3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10·46 × 109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8·63 × 109 per L; neutrophils were 82·4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases—the KPC-2 genotype—had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.
Additionally, antimicrobial susceptibility testing indicated that the K pneumoniae had changed its antimicrobial susceptibility profile: initially it had the characteristic growth of classic KPC-2 (figure), which is susceptible to the ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam-avibactam combinations; and after 3 weeks, the profile had changed to the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae, which is resistant to the ceftazidime-avibactam combination but susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam (figure).
The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid β-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants—although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.
options: blaKPC-2, blaNDM, blaKPC-variant, AmpC

An 85-year-old woman was referred to our department for investigation of unexplained nausea, anorexia, malaise, and weight loss of 7 kg over 3 months. She had a history of mild Alzheimer's dementia. Physical examination was unremarkable—specifically, there were no noteworthy abdominal signs. Repeated measurements of her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) showed moderately raised values ranging from 47 mm/h to 53 mm/h. Full blood count showed she was anaemic with haemoglobin concentrations ranging from 9·5 g/dL to 7·9 g/dL. She also had a neutrophil leucocytosis with values varying between 12·1 × 109 per μL and 17·9 × 109 per μL. The patient's serum C-reactive protein (CRP) varied from 139 mg/L to 170 mg/L. She had low-grade pyrexia 3 days after admission, with her temperature ranging from 37·3°C to 37·9°C. However, no source of sepsis was found after clinical examination. Baseline investigations for exploration of pyrexia or inflammation of unknown origin were undertaken; a chest x-ray, urine and blood cultures, echocardiography, microbial serology, and autoantibody screening were all negative. CT scans of her thorax, abdomen, and pelvis were undertaken to rule out the possibility of an occult tumour or an abscess; they were normal. Values of her ESR and CRP remained elevated and blood cultures were repeatedly negative. As we had drawn a blank in our search for an inflammatory or infective cause of our patient's continuing pyrexia, we decided to do a 18Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan. The 18Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT images showed a marked increase in tracer uptake in the thoracic and abdominal aorta, and the subclavian, carotid, and axillary arteries—consistent with widespread vasculitis. A biopsy of the temporal artery was done, and subsequent histological examination showed a classic picture of giant cell arteritis (GCA). The patient was commenced on oral prednisolone at a daily dose of 1 mg/kg. Within 4 days, her constitutional symptoms had resolved, and she was able to eat regular meals without nausea. Values of her CRP and ESR reverted to normal, and the low-grade pyrexia resolved fully. This case illustrates that GCA can sometimes present with non-specific and atypical features—particularly in patients later in life. Additionally, 18Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT imaging can be highly useful for finding the cause of pyrexia or inflammation that has not been identified using the usual methods of investigation.Figure Searching for a source of inflammation or infection using 18Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan

An 86-year-old man was seen at home by an ambulance crew after a fall associated with sudden severe lower back pain and weakness in his legs. The paramedics reported that they found the patient alert and haemodynamically stable; his legs appeared pale—although the colour returned during the journey to the hospital—and he had weak pedal pulses.On arrival at the emergency department, we also found him to be alert and comfortable. He did not report any breathlessness or chest pain either ongoing or pre-admission.
In his medical history, he had hypertension, diabetes mellitus, prostatic hypertrophy, and atrial fibrillation (AF) and was prescribed amlodipine, tamsulosin, ramipril, and warfarin.
On examination, the patient's vital signs were normal, but he had bilateral flaccid weakness and paraesthesia of his legs, and his right femoral pulse was weaker compared to the left.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a raised blood lactate concentration of 5·5 mmol/L (normal <1·0)—were unremarkable. His electrocardiogram showed rate-controlled AF with no acute changes.
However, a contrast CT scan—examining for traumatic injuries—showed dilatation of the ascending aorta and an extensive Stanford type A aortic dissection with sparing of the coronary ostia and with no pericardial or pleural effusions (appendix). An echocardiogram showed a clear dissection flap, a dilated aortic root, and mild to moderate aortic regurgitation (figure). While we were doing the echocardiogram, fluid started accumulating rapidly in the pericardial space; there were no warning signs or preceding symptoms. The fluid accumulation led to right ventricular and then left ventricular compression and cardiac tamponade resulting in a brief period of a so-called “swinging heart” appearance in the blood-filled, pericardial sac (video). The patient became unresponsive and then had a cardiac arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was unsuccessful.
Ascending aortic dissection presenting solely with the features of spinal cord ischaemia with no chest symptoms is extremely rare: occurring in less than 1% of cases. If unrecognised and untreated, it is invariably catastrophic due to proximal extension of the dissection which can either affect blood flow in the left main stem coronary artery or—as in our patient—result in lethal cardiac tamponade due to aortic rupture. The lower limb weakness resulting from the spinal cord ischaemia is caused by restricted blood flow to the spinal arteries.
Evolving cardiac tamponade—which we believe has not been recorded on transthoracic echocardiogram previously—is a life-threatening emergency that even in a surgical centre has a high mortality. With type A aortic dissection emergency surgery can reduce the 1-month mortality from 90% to 30%. Stringent control of the blood pressure—using intravenous agents such as labetalol—and adequate analgesia are essential while awaiting surgery (video).
target: Stanford type B aortic dissection with retrograde expansion.
options: Anterior spinal cord syndrome due to burst fracture of vertebra., DeBakey type II aortic dissection., Hemi-section of the spinal cord., Stanford type B aortic dissection with retrograde expansion.

A 23-year-old man presented to our centre with a 1-day history of non-exertional shortness of breath. The patient stated that he woke up in the morning with wheezing; he reported no fever, chills, nasal congestions, or productive cough.
The patient had been diagnosed with asthma when he was a child; he had previously needed a hospital admission which required him to be intubated, due to an exacerbation of his illness. Notably, he had never been seen by a respiratory physician, but had previously been treated for pneumonia both as an inpatient and an outpatient. He reported using an inhaler of albuterol daily.
On examination, the patient was initially tachypnoeic on bilevel positive airway pressure with increased respiratory effort and oxygen saturation of 89%; his lungs were clear on auscultation bilaterally with minimal wheezing heard. A chest x-ray showed bilateral opacities and he was admitted for empirical treatment of asthma exacerbation. A CT scan of the patient's chest was requested primarily to assess for parenchymal lung disease; however, it showed an H-type tracheooesophageal fistula at the T3 level, which we concluded was most likely to have been congenital in origin (figure).Upon further questioning, the patient reported no symptoms of dysphagia, frank aspiration, or gastro-oesophageal reflux. Additionally, he had none of the other clinical features of either VACTERL association—specifically vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, renal anomalies, and limb abnormalities—or CHARGE syndrome—specifically coloboma, cranial nerve abnormalities, choanal atresia, and so-called CHARGE ear (middle and inner ear abnormalities, which can contribute to hearing problems, and atypically shaped external ears). An echocardiogram, MRI of the spine, anorectal examination, and renal ultrasounds were all within usual range.
On discussion with the patient, we decided to operate. Bronchoscopy confirmed a fistula (figure) through which a stiff catheter was passed into the oesophagus; the end of the catheter was retrieved via oesophagoscopy and brought back out through the mouth to allow for retraction and identification of the fistula by fluoroscopy (figure). The fistula was divided—closing the tracheal and oesophageal defects—via a right cervical approach. A sternocleidomastoid rotational flap was then interposed between the trachea and oesophagus; intraoperative monitoring of the recurrent laryngeal nerve confirmed that it was undamaged. A postoperative oesophagram showed no fistula recurrence or leak; the patient retained a normal swallowing mechanism, and his voice was unaffected after surgery.
At follow-up 4 months after the operation, the patient was well; he reported no dysphagia or respiratory difficulties. He said he had used his inhaler on one occasion since discharge from hospital.
Congenital tracheooesophageal fistulae are a rare developmental anomaly that may present soon after birth, in infancy, in childhood, or in adulthood—as in our patient. The diagnosis should be considered in patients of any age with unexplained chronic, recurrent respiratory symptoms or cases of suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux.
