A 52-year-old right-handed woman was referred to our clinic reporting a 4-year history of spontaneous unpredictable episodes of dizziness. The patient was seen remotely due to restrictions imposed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. She described the episodes as a sudden sensation of feeling like the room was spinning for 5–40 s; they were happening approximately three times a day and she could identify no triggers. Occasionally, the episodes were associated with nausea and vomiting; they had also caused her to fall but did not result in any impairment of consciousness. The patient reported no visual symptoms, tinnitus, or headache. She was otherwise in good health and took no regular medication.The referral, from the otorhinolaryngology clinic via the family doctor, reported a negative Dix-Hallpike test and failure to improve the patient's symptoms with the Epley manoeuvre. The referrer diagnosed Ménière's disease—a triad of tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss—and prescribed the patient a trial of betahistine, bendroflumethiazide, and prochlorperazine with no benefit.
On remote examination the patient appeared well, although further examination was limited as there was no opportunity to test for nystagmus.
Laboratory investigations, previously arranged by the family doctor, had shown no atypical findings—full blood count, renal profile, and liver function were all within normal range. A brain MRI, which had been done 1 year before our consultation, as part of the initial work-up, showed normal brain parenchyma and ventricular system. We requested a further MRI to include high-resolution axial T2-weighted sequences of the posterior fossa; this showed a prominent left-sided vascular loop extending into the internal auditory meatus and causing compression of the left eighth cranial nerve—consistent with our suspected diagnosis of vestibular paroxysmia (figure). We prescribed the patient carbamazepine and she reported that her symptoms had resolved completely soon after commencing the treatment.
Vestibular paroxysmia is a rare cause of spontaneous, brief, and recurrent attacks of vertigo; episodes can be significantly disabling. The diagnosis—as in our patient—often goes unrecognised for many years. The key features differentiating vestibular paroxysmia from more common causes of vertigo are the spontaneity, the brevity, and the frequency. Regarding spontaneity, attacks are not typically triggered by head movement; syndromes to consider if attacks are triggered by head movement include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, central positional nystagmus (caused by cerebellar and brainstem lesions), and bow hunter syndrome (vertebrobasilar insufficiency resulting from vertebral artery occlusion during neck rotation, usually from cervical spondylosis). Regarding brevity, attacks are usually < 1min; syndromes to consider if episodes are longer include Ménière's disease (typically attacks last 20 min to 12 h) and vestibular migraine (5 min to 72 h). And finally, regarding frequency, attacks occur up to 30 or more times per day; syndromes where episodes are less frequently include vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attacks and epileptic vertigo.
Although infrequently encountered, vestibular paroxysmia is a condition to be aware of since it is an eminently treatable cause of dizziness and could very easily be mistaken for more common causes. MRIs typically show neurovascular compression of the eighth cranial nerve—radiologists should be asked to specifically look for this.
options: Betahistine, Epley manoeuvre, Microvascular decompression surgery of the eighth cranial nerve, Carbamazepine

A 65-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 1-day history of fever and falls, saying that her legs had given out from under her. The patient's symptoms began within 1 day of the first dose of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. She had a medical history of hypertension and diabetes.On examination in the emergency department, the patient's temperature was 39·1°C, her respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min, and her heart rate was 88 beats per min. As she met the criteria for systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), an extensive infection work-up was initiated and she was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Laboratory investigations found a D-dimer concentration of 5267 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 69 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein concentration of 63·4 mg/L. The patient's white blood cell count, lactate, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen panel—including SARS-CoV-2—and urine and blood cultures were unremarkable. Due to concerns of exposure to SARS-CoV-2, the PCR test was repeated after 24 h, but this was again negative.
CT of the patient's chest showed multiple pulmonary nodules measuring up to 1·1 cm. A small filling defect in a distal subsegmental pulmonary artery was also seen, which we thought was inconsistent with an acute pulmonary embolism and probably artifactual. Doppler ultrasounds of the patient's lower limbs were normal; her head CT was also normal.
4 days after presentation, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT was done to characterise the pulmonary nodules; it showed uptake in the fat stranding posterior to the right deltoid (figure); moderately increased uptake within multiple right axillary lymph nodes (figure); and diffusely increased splenic uptake (figure). The pulmonary nodules had no uptake—indicating that they were probably benign.
The patient's symptoms resolved 3 days after the vaccination. Given the imaging findings, the temporal relationship of the symptoms to the vaccination, and negative test results from an extensive work-up for malignant and infectious causes, we believe, the diagnosis was a local and systemic immune response following vaccination. However possible masking effects of broad-spectrum antibiotics cannot be excluded.
The high D-dimer concentration probably reflected significant concomitant coagulation and fibrinolysis associated with SIRS.
The local response was demonstrated by hypermetabolism within the axillary lymph nodes draining the site of intramuscular injection; diffusely increased splenic activity suggests a systemic response—corroborated by elevated inflammatory markers.
As the global vaccination effort continues, more patients will undoubtedly require assessment and investigation shortly after immunisation. Imaging and laboratory findings consistent with a systemic immune response might result in further unnecessary evaluation or interventions. However, findings overlap with other diseases—notably those of the 18F-FDG PET/CT scan in patients with malignancies. Recognition of the clinical and imaging features of the systemic immune response to vaccination might become essential in the coming months (video).

options: Ultrasound of the axillary lymph nodes, Biopsy of the axillary lymph nodes, Peripheral blood flow cytometry, Observation

A 46-year-old woman presented to our outpatient clinic in June, 2013, with frequent collapse, ischaemic scalp ulcerations, and hair loss (figure). She had undergone carotid endarterectomy in 2005, after a small right hemispheric stroke, and had no other medical history apart from hypercholesterolaemia. She had no previous dermatological or scalp problems. She took clopidogrel 75 mg, aspirin 80 mg, and simvastatin 40 mg daily.
Magnetic resonance angiography showed occlusion of both common carotid arteries, the innominate artery, and the right vertebral artery, and 80% stenosis of the orifice of the left subclavian artery. The circle of Willis was perfused by the left vertebral artery, and the right vertebral artery was filled retrograde from the left side. Blood supply to the head was maintained by the stenosed left subclavian artery (figure).
We inserted an 8 × 24 mm balloon-expandable Express stent (Boston Scientific, Natick, MA, USA) to the stenosed left subclavian artery via the left groin (appendix). There were no complications. Postintervention transcranial Doppler showed an increase of 120% in the mean velocity of the left medial cerebral artery, from 40 cm/s to 88 cm/s after stenting.
At follow-up in December, 2013, the patient's dizziness and collapse had resolved. Her scalp lesions were almost healed, and hair growth had normalised (appendix).
Ischaemic scalp lesions due to insufficient tissue perfusion are rare. Most cases of scalp ischaemia are caused by giant cell arthritis, malignancy (angiosarcoma or melanoma), radiotherapy, or inflammation. In our case the cause was treatable with revascularisation of the extracranial arteries.
options: Collapse, Hair loss, Seizures, Dizziness

The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness—persisting for several minutes—followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8–12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11–18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation—related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.
options: Stroke, Vasospasm, Low blood pressure, Embolism

A woman aged 24 years with a history of cerebral infarction presented with eruptions on the acral regions that had relapsed in winter since her childhood. On examination, we observed brownish erythema and dark red scaly papules on the fingers and toes (figure A, B). The patient's younger sister, mother, and maternal grandfather had similar eruptions (figure D, E, F). Magnetic resonance angiography showed multiple cerebral aneurysms in the patient (figure H, I, J). There was no evidence of intellectual disability or basal ganglia calcification. Laboratory tests showed normal blood cell counts and complement: positive for antinuclear antibodies at 1:80, positive for anticardiolipin antibodies at 27·1 IU/mL, and negative for antidouble-stranded DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins. Multiple enlarging cerebral aneurysms and a previous cerebral infarction were found in the patient's younger sister (figure L), although neither anticardiolipin antibodies nor other coagulation abnormalities were detected. The previously reported heterozygous TREX1 (pAsp18Asn) mutation 53G→A was identified in the family and familial chilblain lupus was diagnosed.Chilblain lupus erythematosus is a rare and unique form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus that is characterised by chilblains, which are cold-induced eruptions on the acral regions. A familial form of chilblain lupus erythematosus, related to heterozygous mutations in TREX1 and SAMHD1, has been previously reported. To date, there have been two case reports of familial chilblain lupus that have included cerebral vasculopathy presenting as multiple cerebral aneurysms, narrowing cerebral arteries, or cerebral infarction. Chilblains with family history and systemic symptoms might suggest the presence of hereditary autoinflammatory diseases.
Avoiding cold exposure, applying topical corticosteroid, or taking systemic immunosuppressive agents can be therapeutic options. In this case, administration of systemic prednisolone (1·0 mg/kg per day) improved the acral eruptions and the cerebral aneurysms. Because of the occurrence of hyperlipidaemia, the prednisolone dose was gradually tapered to 5 mg/day. Both the skin and the cerebral lesions have remained stable for 6 months. Familial chilblain lupus can present with various symptoms in a family with identical gene mutations. Recognising that cerebral infarctions and aneurysms can occur in familial chilblain lupus cases is important. Further investigation is needed to better understand the pathomechanisms and to prevent such severe complications.
options: Cryoglobulinemia, Familial chilblain lupus, Dermatomyositis, Fabry disease

A 24-year-old woman was referred to our specialist unit with a 3-month history of 15·8 kg weight loss, increasing abdominal pain and bloating, fatigue, night sweats, difficulty passing urine, amenorrhoea, and trouble walking. She was nulligravida and had a copper intrauterine device (IUD) in situ for the past 4 years. She was a non-smoker, drank alcohol socially, and had no history of recent travel. She stated she was allergic to penicillin.On examination, the patient was pale and cachexic—body-mass index 20·15 kg/m2—and afebrile, with normal vital signs (appendix). She had an abdominopelvic mass of approximately 18-week gestation that was continuous with the cervix, uterus, and anterior abdominal wall.
Investigations showed her human chorionic gonadotropin serum concentration pregnancy test was negative, haemoglobin concentration was 68 g/L (normal 120–160), CA-125 antigen concentration was 152 IU/mL (normal <35 IU/mL) and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was 146 mg/L (normal 0–5). All other blood tests were unremarkable.
Ultrasound, CT, and MRI of the pelvis showed an 18 week-sized uterine mass invading the anterior abdominal wall, bladder, colon, ileum, and enlarged pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes (figure). 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET–CT showed extensive hypermetabolic abnormalities below the diaphragm (appendix). The IUD had partially perforated into the myometrium.
We considered uterine lymphoma, sarcoma, and actinomycosis as differential diagnoses. However, histopathological examination of core biopsies of the mass from two different sites on two separate occasions only showed inflammation—with no histological evidence of malignancy, actinomyces, tuberculosis, or fungal infection.
Culture of core tissue samples, endocervical swabs, and the IUD—which was removed—had no bacterial or fungal growth. Despite this, given the IUD perforation into the myometrium, extensive and contiguous crossing of tissue boundaries, and lack of histological evidence of malignancy, we started treatment for actinomycosis. Initially, we used intravenous ceftriaxone but switched to penicillin—the antibiotic of choice—after hypersensitivity skin testing was negative. To facilitate ambulatory management, treatment was subsequently changed to oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day. The patient's symptoms improved significantly within a week, and 3 months later her CRP concentration had dropped to 0·7 mg/L; imaging showed complete resolution of actinomycosis and her return to good health (appendix).
Actinomycosis is caused by a filamentous, Gram-positive, anaerobic bacteria, Actinomyces spp, which is of low virulence and unable to cross normal mucosal barriers. However, once trauma breaches the mucosa, the organism spreads contiguously, disregarding anatomical planes.
Clinicians should consider the diagnosis of actinomycosis when there is either progression across tissue boundaries or the development of sinus tracts. Confirmation by culture and or histological findings of sulphur granules may be negative; newer techniques such as 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionisation time-of-flight can facilitate the diagnosis. Treatment for 6–12 months is key to preventing relapse. Actinomyces-like organisms are found in the pap smears of approximately 7% of IUD users and pose no risk if there are no signs or symptoms of infection. Injury to myometrium and IUDs left in situ for prolonged periods are risk factors for an actinomycosis infection which, if suspected, warrants removal of the IUD and prompt treatment (video).

A 37-year-old female patient was referred to the rheumatology department at Treliske Hospital (Truro, UK) in April, 2015, following 8 months of rib pain, initially thought to be costochondritis. She had isolated hypophosphataemia (serum phosphate level 0·50 mmol/L) and a pelvic MRI identified stress fractures (figure, A). 14 months after her presentation she had a persistently low serum phosphate concentration, with normal parathyroid hormone and serum calcium levels, and a 25(OH) vitamin D concentration of 32ng/mL. It was concluded that she had subclinical vitamin D deficiency, and she was prescribed cholecalciferol 20 000 units per week and Phosphate Sandoz (HK Pharma Ltd, Bedford UK), given as two tablets twice daily. In March, 2016, still symptomatic, she was referred to the UCL Centre for Nephrology (University College London, London, UK) to investigate a possible renal cause for her hypophosphataemia.There, her calculated urinary fractional excretion of phosphate was raised at 42%, confirming hyperphosphaturia. Her sex and age weighed against X-linked, autosomal dominant, or recessive hypophosphatemic rickets; and normal excretion of low-molecular-weight protein, urate, and glucose ruled out the renal Fanconi syndrome. Her serum concentration of FGF23 was 180 relative units (RU) per mL (normal range is 0–150 RU/mL). Previous standard practice protocolled a first-line FDG PET/CT scan, which identified a nasal cavity mass that was avid on a subsequent 68Ga DOTATATE PET/CT scan (figure B). The tumour was excised and pathology confirmed as sinonasal mucosa with evidence of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; her serum phosphate and FCF23 returned to normal following surgery.
Oncogenic osteomalacia is a paraneoplastic syndrome usually associated with mesenchymal tumours, although somatic mutations in adenocarcinomas causing this syndrome have been reported. Phosphatonins (eg, FGF23) decrease renal resorption of phosphate, leading to hypophosphataemia, muscle weakness, and osteomalacia. Most such tumours are located in the bone and soft tissue, are solitary, and rarely cause local symptoms, often making the diagnosis long and difficult. Use of radiolabelled somatostatin analogues (such as octreotate, as in a 68GA-DOTATATE scan) is the most sensitive and specific functional imaging.
The only definitive management is removal of the phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour; recurrence is rare but has been described in some cases.

options: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, Fanconi syndrome, Oncogenic osteomalacia, Vitamin D deficiency

input:
A 75-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with fatigue and vomiting. She also reported that for the previous 6 months she had muscle weakness, central obesity, and skin fragility. She had a history of dyslipidaemia and hypertension.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile with a temperature of 38°C, her blood pressure was 140/60 mm Hg, and her heart rate between 90 and 100 beats per min. She was cognitively impaired and lethargic.
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated white blood cell count of 11·17 × 109 per L (normal range 4·5–11·5), a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 391·63 mg/L (normal <6), and profound hypokalaemia: serum potassium concentration 1·76 mmol/L (normal 3·5–5).
We started empirical antibiotic treatment with cefoxitin and metronidazole and began an intravenous infusion of potassium chloride. She continued to vomit; her serum potassium concentration remained low and her temperature remained around 38°C, and daily blood glucose levels showed a gradual increase requiring sliding scale insulin.
A CT scan of the patient's thorax and abdomen showed a large mass near the omental bursa (figure) and filling defects in the distal branches of the pulmonary artery, indicating a pancreatic neoplasm with a concurrent pulmonary embolism. Compression ultrasonography with doppler showed a deep venous thrombosis in the patient's left calf; we started her on enoxaparin.
A percutaneous, transgastric, ultrasound-guided biopsy was done and histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen showed a pancreatic adenocarcinoma of low differentiation and pleomorphic giant cells. Immunohistochemistry testing was positive for CK7, MUC1, AE1/AE3, and E-cadherin.
Despite continuous potassium repletion, daily laboratory examinations persistently showed severe hypokalaemia—with average serum potassium concentrations of around 2 mmol/L.
Further exploration of the patient's hypokalaemia found a spot urine potassium concentration of 40·4 mmol/L and a spot urine sodium concentration of 90·9 mmol/L, indicating renal wasting.
Additional investigations found raised plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH; 121·6 pg/mL; normal 4·7–48·8), high cortisol level (51 μg/dL; normal 6·24–18·0), and low levels of thyroid stimulating hormone (0·02 mIU/L; normal 0·5–8·9) in the context of a metabolic alkalosis.
Taken together, the findings indicated a diagnosis of ectopic Cushing's syndrome consistent with an ACTH-secreting pancreatic tumour.
We started treatment with the steroid synthesis inhibitor ketoconazole orally at a dose of 200 mg twice a day. The patient's potassium level returned to normal after 1 month, she was then treated palliatively, and died 3 months later.
Neuroendocrine tumours of the bronchus, lung, thymus, and pancreas, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, and pheochromocytoma are the most frequent sites of ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions, but they can occur in almost every type of neoplasm. The resulting Cushing's syndrome—also known as paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome—usually develops rapidly and has features that are more pronounced: some patients present with purple striae, profound hypokalaemia—as seen in our case—and severe hypertension. The more typical features of Cushing's syndrome—the rounding of the face, and weight gain in the recognised distribution—are unusual in cases caused by ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions. Cushing's syndrome may cause a prothrombotic state and as such is a recognised risk factor for thromboembolic disease. Persistent electrolyte disturbances in combination with such tumours should always raise suspicion of ectopic Cushing's syndrome (video).
output: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma with ectopic Cushing’s syndrome

input: A 59-year-old man came to our hospital saying that he had been accidentally shot by a fellow hunter during an expedition to the local moorland. He was alone when he walked into the department. During physical examination he was found to be asymptomatic and all his vital signs were stable. His blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and he did not complain of any dizziness or shortness of breath. Furthermore, no active bleeding was noted. An emergency whole-body CT (figure) was done and showed that shotgun pellets were evenly distributed in his body—from his knees to his neck—and that some had penetrated internally to affect several organs. A CT scan of his chest also showed that two of the pellets had reached the mediastinum: one had stopped a few millimetres from the floor of the aortic arch (figure), and the other one penetrated the pericardium, stopping between the pericardium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle (figure). A CT angiogram showed that no contrast agent was leaking from around the aorta or pericardium. We also did an echocardiogram, which, except for a small pericardial effusion, indicated that the patient was haemodynamically stable. The CT angiogram was repeated 24 h later, and, fortunately for the patient, nothing significantly had changed. At this stage, there were no indications for cardiac surgery to remove the pellets so—with the patient's agreement—we decided to take no further action after having weighed up the pros and cons of undertaking high-risk cardiac surgery or leaving the pellets where they were. After a few days of observation and antibiotic prophylaxis ceftriaxone (1 g a day for a week), the patient was discharged. He remained symptom free when seen again several months later.Hunting rifles and shotguns use cartridges that contain variable numbers of small pellets. Once the rifle or shotgun is discharged, these tiny projectiles spread out evenly and circumferentially from the barrel to increase the possibility of hitting a target. Judging by the distribution of the pellets on our patient's torso, we surmised that his fellow hunter had shot him from approximately 20 m. In the assessment of such patients, a key consideration is whether any pellets have penetrated vital organs. Furthermore, it is necessary to decide whether to surgically remove the pellets or simply leave them inside the body, where they will eventually be encapsulated in fibrous tissue.
options: Shotgun pellets, Allergic reaction, Widespread tick bites, Cherry Angiomas

input:
A 19-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. He had no medical history. On examination his temperature was 38·8°C, he was dehydrated and tachycardic, and he had postural hypotension: his blood pressure was 110/40 mm Hg supine and 88/36 mm Hg standing. On palpation of his abdomen, the patient reported widespread pain with equivocal rebound tenderness. We also noted diffuse darkening of the mucous membranes and skin, which the patient said had gradually increased over the past 7 years. The hyperpigmentation was more pronounced on the skin over the patient's joints, hands and feet nail beds, gingivae, and the dorsum of the tongue (figure).Laboratory tests showed a sodium concentration of 116 mmol/L, a potassium concentration of 5·3 mmol/L, a low morning serum cortisol concentration of 63·4 nmol/L (normal range 172–496), and a high plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration of 440 pmol/L (normal range 1·5–13·9). We started the patient on an intravenous saline drip and gave him a bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone intravenously. After 24 h the patient's symptoms improved, and after 6 days his electrolytes normalised.
Further investigations found no HIV antibodies, no antibodies against 21-hydroxylase, no antibodies to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (also known as South American blastomycosis), and a negative tuberculin test. However, the patient's serum concentration of hexacosanoic acid—a very long chain fatty acid (VLCFA)—was 2·82 μmol/L (normal range 0·22–0·88).
Molecular sequencing found a missense mutation in exon 6 of the ABCD1 gene—the R518Q mutation—in both the patient and his mother confirming the diagnosis of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Additionally, when we repeated a neurological examination, we found the patient to have a previously unnoticed, slight left hemiparesis with preserved deep tendon reflexes, muscle tone, and normal sensation. After 9 days in the hospital, the patient went home taking oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.
The characteristic mucocutaneous manifestations of Addison's disease (AD) are the crucial clue in diagnosing this life-threatening condition: ideally, they should be engrained into every clinician's visual memory—the other signs and symptoms of AD are non-specific.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a rare genetic disorder characterised by intracellular accumulation of VLCFA. Phenotypes range from a severe progressive cerebral form in boys to a myelopathy form in adults. AD may occur throughout the lifespan, independently of the neurological presentations; it is seen as an isolated manifestation in up to 10% of cases. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy must be considered as a differential diagnosis of AD in young men—even if neurological symptoms are not obvious at initial examination, as we found in our patient (video).
options: Lead poisoning, Acute intermittent porphyria, Adrenal insufficiency, Hemochromatosis

input:
A 62-year-old male with psoriatic arthritis, chronic pancreatitis, and alcohol-related liver disease presented with 3 days of increasing breathlessness, chest discomfort, and non-productive cough 2 weeks after admission for acute-on-chronic alcohol-induced pancreatitis (managed conservatively). Examination was pertinent for tachypnoea 28 breaths per min, 1 L/min oxygen requirement, and absent breath sounds on auscultation over the right hemithorax. His abdomen was soft and non-tender. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (15·4 × 109/L), elevated C-reactive protein (65 mg/L), hypoalbuminaemia (27 g/L), deranged liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase 166 units [U]/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 267 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 62 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L) and hyperlipasaemia (1720 U/L). Chest radiography showed a massive right-sided pleural effusion (figure A). Intercostal catheter insertion provided symptomatic relief following initial drainage of 1550 mL haemoserous effusate. Pleural fluid analysis confirmed an exudative process, elevated concentrations of amylase (19 224 U/L) and lipase (88 220 U/L), and a normal triglyceride level (0·4 mmol/L). Culture and cytology were negative.
The pleural aspirate was sent for pancreatic enzyme quantification on admission, acknowledging the recent bout of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis as a major clue to a pancreaticopleural fistula. Early contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen identified multiple pancreatic calcifications (consistent with sequelae of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis) and a retroperitoneal fluid collection posterior to the pancreatic body (figure B). Subsequent pancreatic magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) identified a communication between the peripancreatic collection and right pleural cavity, confirming a pancreaticopleural fistula (figure B and C). No pancreatic duct strictures or dilatations were seen. The patient was successfully managed with alcohol abstinence, dietary optimisation, and continued intercostal catheter drainage, enabling spontaneous fistula closure without the need for advanced endoscopic or surgical intervention. Care was complicated by the interval development of meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus empyema in a previously sterile pleural fluid, necessitating antibiotics and intrapleural lysis. Follow-up imaging confirmed resolution of the fistula and the patient remains well without recurrent pancreatitis or pleural effusion 17 months after discharge.
Pancreaticopleural fistula is a rare yet serious complication of pancreatitis, with an estimated incidence of 0·4%. A high index of suspicion is essential to avoid delay in diagnosis and treatment. The classic presentation is a male, typically in their fourth or fifth decade of life, with a history of alcohol misuse and new onset breathlessness following an episode of pancreatitis. Abdominal features are infrequent. Unlike small reactive effusions in acute pancreatitis, effusions of this nature tend to be massive and recurrent, and although they show a predilection for the left hemithorax, there are increasing reports of right-sided and bilateral involvement. Thoracentesis typically reveals an exudative straw-coloured to serosanguinous fluid rich in amylase, lipase, or both. Assessment of pancreatic enzymes is highly cost-effective and virtually diagnostic in this context. Further, MRCP is the imaging modality of choice to unveil a fistulous tract, offering sensitivity of up to 80%. In the absence of significant pancreatic ductal pathology, medical therapy can be considered as the first-line approach, including pleural drainage to alleviate respiratory symptoms and restore pleural apposition, and somatostatin analogues to reduce pancreatic secretions. Recognising empyema as a potential complication of an otherwise necessary intervention emphasises the importance of rigorous intercostal catheter drainage site hygiene, especially given anticipated long dwell times (to combat enduring pancreatic fluid production) and heightened risk of infection in a stereotypical chronic alcohol-dependent and malnourished cohort. Endoscopic intervention with sphincterotomy or pancreatic duct stenting to divert fluid towards the duodenum might be considered on anatomical grounds, or if there is an inadequate response to medical management. Surgery is generally reserved for patients who are unresponsive to medical or endoscopic therapy.
options: Hepatic hydrothorax, Reactive effusion due to pancreatitis, Pancreaticopleural fistula, Malignant pleural effusion

input: A 15-year-old girl presented with short stature; her height was 1·42 m (3 cm below third percentile) and her bodyweight was 41·8 kg (around 50th percentile). She had a round face and several subcutaneous nodules over her forehead, hands, and knees. She had hypoplasia of her fourth and fifth metacarpals bilaterally (figure). Serum calcium and parathormone concentrations were normal. Genetic testing showed that she was heterozygous for a non-sense mutation affecting GNAS, confirming the diagnosis of pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. GNAS encodes the α-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is indicative of genomic imprinting. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. Brachydactyly is due to premature closure of the epiphyses in the metacarpals.
options: Turner's syndrome, Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, Pseudohypoparathyroidism, Renal failure

input: A 62-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of low back pain and a 1-day history of lethargy. Physical examination was notable for tenderness over the lumbar spine and a normal neurologic examination. Radiographs of the lumbar spine showed gas within L4. Computed tomography of the lumbar spine confirmed the presence of intramedullary gas within L4, and also showed that the gas extended into the surrounding soft tissue, epidural space, and psoas muscles. What is the most likely etiology of this skeletal finding?

1. Air embolism
2. Calcium oxalate crystal deposition

A 52-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic for evaluation of several bluish nodules of the right hand and wrist (figure) that had gradually increased in number over the previous 31 years. The lesions were asymptomatic but had been causing the patient embarrassment and had started affecting his social interactions. No one in his family had a history of similar lesions. During adolescence he had had surgical excision of several painful enchondromas involving the proximal phalanx of the right fifth finger and three chondrosarcomas of the metacarpo-phalangeal joints of the right hand, but at the time he had no evidence of cutaneous lesions and therefore had been diagnosed as having Ollier disease (enchondromatosis).On examination he had several hard, painless, compressible, angiomatous, subcutaneous nodules on the fingers of the right hand, consistent with a diagnosis of enchondromas, which was confirmed on radiography (figure). Histology of one of the skin lesions showed typical features of cavernous haemangioma—ie, large blood-filled spaces lined by tumour endothelial cells separated by fibrous tissue. Human herpesvirus type 8 and D2-40 immunohistochemical stains were negative. On the basis of clinical and histological findings we made a diagnosis of Maffucci syndrome. We referred the patient to our plastic surgery department for excision of the largest angiomas, and he has follow-up every 6 months to assess new or changing lesions and check for possible chondrosarcomas.
Maffucci syndrome is a rare, sporadic genodermatosis affecting both males and females, which is associated with postzygotic somatic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 genes. Although cases of late-onset Maffucci syndrome have been reported, it usually manifests around age 4–5 years, affecting the hands or feet in a unilateral or asymmetrical fashion. Clinically, it is characterised by the combination of benign enlargements of cartilage (enchondromas) and multiple angiomatous skin lesions—usually cavernous haemangiomas, but patients can also present with lymphangiomas and spindle cell haemangioendotheliomas. Treatment is usually necessary only for aesthetic or functional problems. Surgery is the most common therapeutic approach for both cartilaginous and cutaneous lesions. Possible complications include spontaneous fractures, malignant transformation of angiomatous lesions, and sarcomatous degeneration of enchondromas—with a lifetime risk of about 100%. Prompt identification of Maffucci syndrome can help to identify and treat possible chondrosarcomas in a timely fashion. The principal differential diagnoses are Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Kaposi sarcoma, glomuvenous malformations, Proteus syndrome, blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome, and Ollier disease, which is frequently confused with Maffucci syndrome. Ollier disease does not present with angiomatous lesions but only enchondromas, which have a much lower risk of malignant transformation (about 25% of cases) compared with patients who have Maffucci syndrome.
options: Kaposi Sarcoma, Ollier disease, Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, Maffucci syndrome

input: A 17-year-old girl presented with a 1-month history of pruritic genital lesions. Three months before presentation, she had unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple male partners. On exam, multiple smooth, grayish-white papules and plaques were noted on the vulva and upper inner thighs. The lesions had a smooth, moist appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?

input:
An 80-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of acute-onset severe polyarthralgia of the hands, feet, elbows, and shoulders with associated swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet. The patient had a preceding history of anorexia and weight loss for 2 months associated with fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B–D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24–48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease—especially a malignancy—should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20–50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 75-year-old man with suspected scleral thinning was referred to our ophthalmology clinic. The patient had visited his ophthalmologist in private practice reporting a 10-month history of bilateral, pigmented changes in his sclera.
The patient had a history of severe arthrosis involving several of his joints—including both his shoulders, spine, and both knees and hips—starting in his 60s; he had bilateral total knee endoprostheses of his left knee, aged 70 years, and aged 73 years of the right. He also had physiotherapy treatment. A report when the patient, aged 70 years, had the total knee replacement of his left knee described a deep black discolouration of the cartilage, menisci, and quadriceps tendon.
Additionally, he reported a previous Achilles tendon rupture, dilatative and obliterative arteriopathies—including an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm, which was diagnosed incidentally, resulting in an infrarenal aortic prosthesis at aged 73 years. Also, aged 73 years, the patient was diagnosed with coronary artery sclerosis which did not require treatment; he was found to have peripheral arterial disease. Finally, the patient had prostate stones aged 73 years which were diagnosed after he reported difficulties with micturition; he had a transurethral resection of his prostate.
On examination, the patient was generally well; ophthalmology examination found nasal and temporal dark scleral discoloration on both eyes (figure), with full visual acuity, unremarkable anterior and posterior segments, and normal scleral thicknesses on ultrasound biomicroscopy anterior to the horizontal recti muscles (0·53 mm; typical range 0·4–0·6 equatorial). Coincidentally, we found that both the patient's ear cartilages appeared dark (figure).
Considering the patient's medical history and our findings in the clinic, we suspected a diagnosis of alkaptonuria and referred him to the hospital's clinic for metabolic diseases.
A 24-h urine sample was collected and analysed at the clinic for metabolic diseases; homogentisic acid urine concentration was 9350 mmol/mol creatinine (normal range <30 mmol/mol creatinine). The patient was informed about the diagnosis; his three sons and grandchildren, who have also reported difficulties with their joints, were recommended to have diagnostic testing for alkaptonuria.
The patient was advised to adhere to a low protein diet and was referred to nutritional specialists; he was also referred to the angiology department for reassessment of his peripheral arterial disease. Finally, cost approval for treatment with nitisinone was requested, approved, and started 5 months later.
Alkaptonuria is a rare, autosomal recessive protein metabolism disorder with deficient homogentisate 1,2 dioxygenase, an enzyme that breaks down tyrosine coded for by the HGD gene. Ochronosis describes the accumulation process of homogentisic acid as pigmented deposits in connective tissues; large joints, the cardiovascular system—including heart valves and the intima of vessels; the urogenital system, the skin, and the eyes may be affected, leading to tissue or organ dysfunction and significantly impacting the quality of life. Treatment requires multidisciplinary collaboration, which comprises pain management, physiotherapy, and treating secondary complications such as osteoporosis or osteoarthrosis. Nitisinone, a triketone herbicide—approved for the treatment of inborn errors of tyrosine metabolism, such as hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1—has been shown to decrease urinary and serum homogentisic acid levels and thus may offer a biochemical cure for alkaptonuria; adverse effects of nitisinone include keratopathy or more severe systemic effects such as porphyria, leukocytopenia, or thrombocytopenia.

A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diverticulosis presented to our emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, lower abdominal pain, on his left side, associated with nausea. He did not report any other symptoms: dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, haematuria, fever, or diarrhoea.His vital signs were all normal except that he was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 187/104 mm Hg. A physical examination—including a cardiac examination—found no abnormalities. His white blood cell count was 9 × 109 per L. His blood creatinine concentration was 0·8 mg/dL, and his liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransaminase was 28 IU/L and alanine aminotransaminase was 20 IU/L. A urinalysis showed 1+ protein, one white blood cell, and four red blood cells— thus within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular complexes and variable P wave morphology in lead II with a mean duration of 133 ms and an amplitude of less than 0·25 mV. A non-contrast abdominal CT showed no calculi in the urinary tract. An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was done because of concerns about acute diverticulitis and intestinal ischaemia; this showed acute infarctions in the left kidney and spleen. Although the admission ECG was non-specific, the patient was started on anticoagulant medication, enoxaparin sodium injection 120 mg/day, because of a high index of suspicion that the infarctions were probably caused by cardioembolic events. Subsequently, continuous cardiac telemetry showed that the patient had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation—confirmed with an ECG the next morning. An echocardiogram showed that all 4 chambers of the heart were of normal sizes with a left atrium dimension of 3·8 cm. There were no signs of valvular disease, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%, and a bubble study was negative. Interestingly, the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score was four based on his age, hypertension, and thromboembolic events: 1 point for age 65–74 years, 1 point for a history of hypertension, and 2 points for the current embolic event. The patient's symptoms quickly improved, and he was discharged 3 days later in normal sinus rhythm on anticoagulants enoxaparin sodium 120 mg/day injection and warfarin 7·5 mg/day. Acute renal and splenic infarctions are rare and atrial fibrillation should be suspected as the cause even in the absence of arrhythmia on ECG. Other less frequent causes of renal and splenic infarctions include cancer and subacute bacterial endocarditis. Our case demonstrates that acute renal and splenic infarctions can manifest as the first and only presentation of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation even in the absence of arrhythmia on the ECG. For patients presenting with acute renal and splenic infarction, a work-up should include exploration for underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and an underlying malignancy.

input: An otherwise healthy 45-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of gradual visual loss in both eyes. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral—predominantly peripheral—corneal deposits of numerous minute, crystalline materials (figure A and B). The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. A clinical diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy was made on the basis of shimmering and polychromatic corneal deposits. Serum IgG concentration was 30·3 g/L (normal 8·1–16·9 g/L) and serum electrophoresis showed a monoclonal gammopathy involving IgG-kappa light chain. Our patient was referred to a haematologist and IgG-kappa multiple myeloma was diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. Treatment was initiated with thalidomide, and no ocular-specific drugs were prescribed. During the 7-year follow-up, while maintained on a low-dose thalidomide, our patient was regularly followed up and her vision remained stable. Although still present, the amount of these corneal crystalline deposits appeared to be decreasing and migrate away from the peripheral corneas (figure C and D).
options: Keratitis, Multiple corneal foreign bodies, igG-kappa monoclonal gammopathy, Corneal granular dystrophy

input:
An 83-year-old man was admitted to our hospital reporting a 3-week history of cough and exertional dyspnoea. At the time of admission, the patient was 4 weeks into a 6-week course of daptomycin and rifampicin because he had an infected prosthetic knee joint; he also had a history of pituitary hypoplasia and had not been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.On examination, he was afebrile, his vital signs were normal, and there was no sign of active infection in the prosthetic knee joint.
Laboratory investigations showed a long-standing lymphopenia of 0·7 × 109 cells per L (normal 1·5–4·0) and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 186·5mg/L (normal 0–5). The patient's eosinophil cell count was 0·3 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·4), haemoglobin concentration 97 g/L (normal 130–170), and platelet cell count was 322 × 109 per L (normal 150–400). RT-PCR of four consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were negative; routine sputum culture and sensitivity, tuberculosis work-up, respiratory viral screen, and HIV serology were all negative.
Chest imaging—both x-ray and CT—showed bilateral, predominantly peripheral pulmonary infiltrates (figure).
The patient was initially treated as presumed PCR-negative COVID-19 and the antibiotics were replaced with ceftriaxone; dexamethasone was not indicated because he was not hypoxic.
On day 7, due to persisting cough, a bronchoscopy was done; examination of the washings showed an eosinophilic infiltrate. A diagnosis of acute eosinophilic pneumonitis (AEP) was established through the modified Philit criteria: a respiratory illness of less than 1 month duration, pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, an eosinophilia of at least 25% in bronchoscopic washings, and the exclusion of other pulmonary eosinophilic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and vasculitis. We thought parasitic infections were unlikely to be the cause—given the absence of a peripheral blood eosinophilia or any history of travel to a country where such infections are endemic. Additionally, the patient had no occupational or lifestyle exposure risk factors. And finally, x-ray and CT findings were not suggestive of fungal infections or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. The patient responded rapidly to high dose prednisolone and was allowed home 14 days after he was admitted. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's chest x-ray was normal.
Common causes of AEP include inhaled toxins—such as smoking, inhalational drugs, and dust—medications, and parasitic and fungal infections. Daptomycin therapy is a well recognised cause of eosinophilic pneumonitis, and we believe this was the most likely cause in our case.
Notably, the patient's symptoms, biochemical, and radiological findings—including lymphopenia, raised CRP, and bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates—pointed towards a diagnosis of PCR-negative COVID-19. Clinicians need to be on the look out for those subtle nuances that might indicate alternative diagnoses.
options: Eosinophilic pneumonitis, Cryptogenic organising pneumonia, Mesothelioma, Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis

input:
A 13-year-old boy with a history of fatigue, facial and lower limb oedema, and an intermittent cough was seen at our institution for further evaluation and intervention.
The patient had previously been diagnosed with chylothorax—which had presented with fussiness and respiratory distress when he was an infant; the difficulties had resolved with a low-fat diet. Additionally, the patient was autistic and had a history of poor weight gain with restrictive eating behaviours.
At age 8 years, the bilateral pleural effusions recurred despite the low-fat diet; lymphatic imaging showed thoracic duct obstruction with diffuse lymphatic collateralisation in the mediastinum and lungs. Intervention at that stage resulted in disruption of the thoracic duct and increasing chylothorax; whole exome sequencing demonstrated two missense variants of PIEZO1 (c.5190G>T[p.Trp1730Cys], paternal, uncertain significance), and (c.5947G>C[p.Gly1983Arg], maternal, uncertain significance). At the time, the patient was transferred to our institution for lymphatic evaluation and intervention. The patient had dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance lymphangiography—when contrast medium into lymphatic vessels—which demonstrated central conducting lymphatic anomaly, with bilateral pulmonary lymphatic perfusion via branches of the thoracic duct, dilated paraspinal lymphatic networks, and hepatopulmonary connections.
Selective embolisation of the hepatopulmonary connections and peribronchial lymphatic networks was undertaken using n-butyl cyanoacrylate glue to abolish lymphatic flow to the pleural spaces and lung parenchyma.
The patient had multiple percutaneous lymphatic embolisation procedures and mechanical pleurodesis over the following 12 months, with recurrent pleural effusions, particularly of the right hemithorax.
At age 9 years, after surgical pleurodesis and repeated selective lymphatic embolisation, the pleural effusions stabilised in size becoming chronic and loculated on medical therapy of furosemide and sirolimus. Further genetic testing of lymphatic fluid collected from the thoracic duct during the various interventions demonstrated a somatic PIK3CA variant (c.3140A>T[p.His1047Leu], pathogenic, 1·25% lymphatic endothelium CD31+), prompting transition of sirolimus therapy to alpelisib—an oral, selective alpha-specific PI3K inhibitor.
At age 13 years, after 3 years of intermittently being admitted to hospital with weight loss, exacerbations of dyspnoea, and an alpelisib-related thyroiditis, the patient had increasing fatigue and respiratory distress; pulmonary function testing indicated severe restrictive lung disease.
On examination, we found diminished lung aeration and significant lymphoedema of the abdomen and lower limbs. A chest x-ray showed mild pulmonary oedema and an increase in the size of the right pleural effusion; repeat dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance lymphangiography showed extensive pulmonary lymphatic perfusion and a small thoracic duct (figure). Direct lymphangiography and embolisation with ethiodized oil—injected into a single capsular lymphatic channel—perfused the pleural spaces bilaterally, the mediastinum, and the thoracic duct (figure). The patient was able to tolerate the procedure well and had no acute complications. And at follow-up 3 months later, he reported no cough or active respiratory symptoms, and reduction of the fatigue. A chest x-ray showed a decrease in the size of the right pleural effusion and his pulmonary function testing remained stable.
Central conducting lymphatic anomaly is a heterogeneous form of a group of disorders, known as complex lymphatic anomalies, that encompasses any condition affecting the thoracic duct and cisterna chyli—the primary structures of the central lymphatic system. Leaks or dilations of the thoracic duct or cisterna chyli or associated lymphatic collateral networks can result in pleural effusions, ascites, anasarca, fetal hydrops, protein losing enteropathy, or lymphoedema.
The most common genetic causes of central conducting lymphatic anomaly are RASopathies with pathogenic variants upregulating the RAS/MAPK signalling pathway. Variants in PIEZO1 are associated with generalised lymphatic dysplasia.
Interventions—including selective embolisation of lymphatic channels from the central lymphatic system or direct hepatopulmonary connections, as in our patient—can be effective in quelling the leak of lymphatic fluid into potential spaces such as the pleural cavity or airways.

A 59-year-old man attended our emergency department reporting a sudden onset of a severe headache and photophobia. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient appeared unwell and was covering his eyes with his hands; his blood pressure was 180/90 mm Hg and his heart rate 90 beats per min. He had neck stiffness and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were positive. He had no other neurological deficits and his consciousness was unaffected.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed a diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage predominantly in the basal cisterns (figure). CT angiography showed a left posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm.
The patient was transferred to the neuroradiology department for embolisation; percutaneous left vertebral artery angiography, accessed through the femoral artery, confirmed an irregularly shaped saccular aneurysm along the proximal aspect of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (figure).
During three-dimensional (3D) rotational angiography, we noticed that, after a bolus injection of contrast agent, a large amount of it appeared to have extravasated from an aneurysmal lump—indicative of an aneurysm rupture (figure; video). We urgently proceeded to measurements using 3D rotational angiography, microcatheter placement, and then endovascular coiling. The final angiography showed near complete obliteration of the source of the leak with a small neck remnant (figure). A CT scan showed contrast extravasation in the basal cisterns, but no compressing haematoma or hydrocephalus (figure).
After the procedure, the patient was extubated in the operating room; he was then monitored and cared for on the neurovascular intensive care unit. His postoperative course was excellent, and he was allowed home 10 days later.
Follow-up was planned for 6 months after the surgery, when the aneurysm was to be assessed by repeating an angiogram.
Patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage must be diagnosed and treated in a timely manner to ensure best outcomes. About 70% present with headache, of which 50% present with the so-called thunderclap headache. Notably, headache is the only symptom in about half of all cases; nausea, vomiting, and loss of consciousness may also be present.
Rebleeding—and indeed rupture—is an important complication of cerebral aneurysms, occurring in 8–23% of cases within 72 h, of which 50–90% occur within the first 6 h, which can result in severe brain damage or death. Rebleeding has a mortality of 20–60%. Rebleeding or rupture on the table or during operation is not an unusual occurrence. Risk factors for rebleeding include a poor neurological grade, admission hypertension, and a large aneurysm; the use of antiplatelet drugs may also be associated.
The high mortality rate and the relatively frequent complication of rebleeding indicate that aneurysm repair—either by clipping or inserting a coil—should be carried out as soon as possible after presentation. Guidelines recommend intervention as early as possible or within 72 h in all but the most severe cases.

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11·4 g/dL; normal 12–16), serum creatinine concentration was 1·34 mg/dL (normal 0·6–1·5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1·73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs—indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities—ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus—and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2·4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0·7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care—including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids—and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3·7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1·73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1·3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment—including end stage renal disease or AKI—when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1·73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration—in the absence of other causes of AKI—is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days—although is it usually cleared within 24–72 h after the injury.
In patients with residual renal function, management is conservative, and outcomes are usually favourable. In patients receiving renal replacement therapy, contrast is cleared through dialysis.
Intravenous contrast used in any clinical setting can result in contrast-associated AKI and debate continues over the level of toxicity of currently used materials. In patients with severe chronic kidney disease or receiving renal replacement therapy risks are greater: here the benefits of imaging should be weighed against the potential harm of the contrast (video).

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 1·5 cm large eroded, symptom-less nodule below the right nostril, which had developed over 6 weeks (figure, A). She complained about slightly dry coughing for several months and noted dexter submandibular and cervical lymphadenopathy for 4 weeks. 3 days before admission, progressing dyspnoea, fever, dizziness, and night sweats occurred. Chest radiograph showed mediastinal widening and atelectasis of left upper lobe, CT scan showed massive left cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and bronchoscopy extensive inflammation of trachea and main bronchi causing ruptures. Histopathology showed necrotising granulomatous mediastinitis. Periodic acid-Schiff staining from skin and mediastinal lesions showed 2–4 μm oval microconidia suspicious for Histoplasma capsulatum (figure, B; inset shows microconidium).
Diagnosis of chronic progressive disseminated histoplasmosis was confirmed by tissue PCR analyses and raised specific serum antibody titres. The patient was treated with intraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 16 months under which the skin lesion and pulmonary symptoms resolved completely without any recurrence. She probably became infected 6–12 months before presentation during a 6-month visit to Brazil. Although the patient was HIV negative and not immunocompromised, her asthma treatment containing budesonide might have caused local immunosuppression in the lungs allowing progression of histoplasmosis in an immunocompetent individual.

input: A 76-year-old man with an extremely high serum ferritin concentration (33 790 μg/L) was referred to the National Reference Laboratory for further laboratory testing to determine the cause. Pathology confirmed renal insufficiency and liver damage, with an exceptionally high bilirubin concentration of 730 μmol/L and an unconjugated bilirubin concentration of 272 μmol/L. This light microscopy smear showed that most of the red blood cells have a changed morphology (figure). Scanning electron microscopy, by which high magnifications of the red blood cells can be viewed, showed that the cells form pointed extensions with large membrane pores (figure). This abnormality is not seen in red blood cells from healthy individuals (figure). We suggest that the presence of the H63D haemochromatosis-associated allele is partly the cause of the exceptionally high serum ferritin concentrations, which brings about the abnormal red blood cell morphology.

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs—specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7·9 to 17·7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13·6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes—although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements—usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus—which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

input:
A 21-year-old man presented to the Lausanne University Hospital (CHUV) in August, 2020, with reddened skin lesions on the forehead and upper torso, clinically suggestive of skin lymphoma. Skin biopsy, bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy, and PET-CT with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) subsequently led to a diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, of mature T-cell phenotype, with skin infiltration. After diagnosis, the patient was enrolled in the GRAAL-2014/T clinical trial (NCT02619630).The patient also had type 1 diabetes and was on insulin-pump therapy. He had interrupted his insulin infusion (basal and bolus) for 48 h because of frequent hypoglycaemia. Initial laboratory values showed glucose of 6·5 mmol/L (117 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7·28, lactate 11·8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L), and high concentrations of ketones bodies, consistent with euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
PET scan images (figure) showed both entities: intense 18F-FDG uptake in the acute lymphoblastic leukaemia-infiltrated scalp (maximum standardised uptake value [SUV] 15·2), and reduced brain 18F-FDG uptake (SUV 4·7) indicative of ketone body metabolism. Intravenous insulin with glucose, fluid, and electrolyte replacement, led to the resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis within 48 h; lactatemia fully normalised with chemotherapy (oral prednisone [60 mg/m2 per day on days 1–14]; intravenous vincristine [2 mg per day on days 1, 8, 15, and 22]; intravenous daunorubicin [50 mg/m2 per day on days 1–3 and 30 mg/m2 per day on days 15 and 16]; intravenous cyclophosphamide [750mg/m2 per day on days 1 and 15]; and intravenous L-asparaginase [6000 UI/m2 per day on days 8, 10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 26, and 28]). PET scan obtained after the first induction (appendix) showed haematological remission (confirmed by marrow examination) and restored brain glucose metabolism.
Causes of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis involve processes that impair hepatic glycogen storage or cause glucose consumption or wasting, such as sodium-glucose-transporter-2 inhibitor induced glycosuria or foetal glucose consumption in late-term pregnancy. To our knowledge, this is the first report of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis caused by high glucose uptake in aggressive neoplasia. Tumour aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect), further contributed to metabolic acidosis through lactate release.
With mild symptoms and normal glucose concentration, euglycaemic ketoacidosis might be overlooked. Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis can accompany high-grade haematological malignancy, where 18F-FDG PET shows both diagnoses. Haemato-oncologists should be aware of this presentation in diabetic patients to expedite diagnosis and avoid detrimental delay in management.

input: A previously healthy 76-year-old woman was assessed preoperatively prior to hip arthroplasty. Cardiac examination was notable for a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex—appreciable only in the supine position. She had no signs or symptoms of heart failure. The patient's N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide blood concentration was normal (71 pg/mL). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved biventricular systolic function, unimpaired diastolic relaxation, normal left atrial dimensions free of any intra-atrial septation, and no valvular abnormalities. However, both apical four-chamber and short-axis views showed evidence of extrinsic compression of the left atrium (figure; video 1). A subsequent CT scan identified large, beaked, osseous outgrowths from the thoracic spinal bodies T7 to T10 that were directly compressing the heart's left atrium (figure; video 2). No intervention was recommended in view of the patient's asymptomatic clinical status and she was medically cleared for the orthopaedic surgery.Extrinsic compression of the left atrium is a potential source of distorted blood flow during the cardiac cycle and a rare cause of mid-diastolic apical murmurs. Spinal osteophytes are a recognised source of external compression of mediastinal structures and exert their greatest compressive effect in the supine position due to the weight of the heart falling directly on to the vertebral column. As the degree of obstruction varies with the patient's position, flow turbulence and the consequent murmur may change dynamically while moving from a supine to a semirecumbent position. In contrast to other causes of mid-diastolic murmur—such as mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, atrial myxoma, or cor triatriatum—increasing murmur intensity in recumbency may suggest extrinsic compression as the underlying aetiology.
options: Mitral stenosis, Atrial myxoma, Extrinsic atrial compression, Cortriatriatum

input:
A 19-year-old man presented to our emergency department with abdominal pain and jaundice. He had emigrated from Senegal during infancy. He was found to be a carrier of hepatitis B virus, with a hepatitis B surface antigen serum DNA concentration persistently below 2000 IU/mL. He was negative for hepatitis B e antigen and positive for anti-hepatitis B e antibodies.Laboratory investigations showed severe hepatocellular damage: total bilirubin 35 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 23 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 544 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 971 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 238 U/L. He was anaemic, with a haemoglobin of 8·9 g/dL. The platelet count was slightly reduced at 144 × 109 per L (normal range 150 × 109 to 400 × 109 per L). Abdominal CT showed transient contrast-enhanced areas in the liver during the arterial phase (figure). Liver histology showed enlarged sinusoids containing sickle-cell thrombi (figure). Sickle-cell disease was confirmed by a peripheral blood smear and cellulose acetate electrophoresis with haemoglobin S making up 87% of his haemoglobin.
Additionally, a diagnosis of acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection was made after serum IgM anti-HAV antibodies were detected; IgG anti-HAV seroconversion followed. Serum hepatitis B virus DNA was 1520 IU/mL and hepatitis D virus—also known as hepatitis delta virus—markers were negative. The patient was treated with exchange transfusion of red cells. He made a full clinical recovery and imaging of his liver showed that it had returned to normal. He was discharged 10 days after admission; at that stage, his total bilirubin concentration was 9·3 mg/dL and direct bilirubin was 6·1 mg/dL. 3 months after the original episode, his haemoglobin was stable at a concentration above 10·5 g/dL. His direct bilirubin concentration was 0·23 mg/dL.
Life-threatening hepatic damage can result from sickle-cell sequestration in the liver. Onset of the symptoms—also known as right upper quadrant syndrome—is frequently associated with an infection, with hepatitis or tuberculosis being common causes. In this case, this was our patient's first sickling crisis—previously, he had been asymptomatic—and it is likely that it was triggered by the infection with HAV. Abnormal hepatic perfusion seen during CT scanning can be interpreted as a sign of sinusoidal obstruction. Liver disease is fairly common in sickle-cell disease and includes several intrahepatic disorders that cause occlusion of blood vessels; they can occur when the patient is not in a sickle-cell crisis. Sequestration of sickle cells occurs more frequently in the spleen, with splenic sequestration crises being the presenting symptom in up to 20% of patients with sickle-cell disease. They are more common in childhood and can cause acute anaemia or hypovolaemic shock due to the pooling of large quantities of red blood cells.
