input: A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 1-month history of continuous chest pain, which was worse with movement and on application of pressure to the anterior chest wall. Physical examination showed a pustule on the sole of his left foot (figure A) and multiple pustules on his palms (figure B). Blood analysis, chest radiography, and ECG results were normal. Microscopy and culture for bacteria of the pustules was negative, as was serology for Treponema pallidum and HIV. Immunological tests were done, but no abnormalities were found. A radioisotope scan showed intense activity at the sternoclavicular and first sternocostal joints (figure C). A diagnosis of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome was made. Treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatories and methotrexate was started, resulting in clinical improvement. SAPHO syndrome is characterised by the variable association of osteoarticular manifestations, mainly on the anterior chest wall, and various dermatological conditions—in particular palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne.
options: Pustular psoriasis, SAPHO, Secondary syphilis, Disseminated gonococcal infection

input:
A 36-year-old man with a 6-month history of asthenia, impotence, loss of libido, polyuria, and polydipsia attended our department; he also reported needing to wake up twice at night to urinate and Raynaud's phenomenon. The patient had a medical history of minor anxiety episodes and was prescribed prazepam.
On examination, his weight was 69 kg, height 1·79 m with a BMI of 24·1 kg/m2; the patient stated he had recently lost 5 kg. Significant muscle atrophy and a reduction of body hair was noted; his pulse was 72 beats per min, blood pressure 124/77 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97%. He had noticeable lymphadenopathy of cervical and inguinal nodes. Neurological examination was normal—he had no disturbance of his vision.
Laboratory investigations showed total testosterone concentration of 0·12 ng/mL (normal level >1·65) with follicle-stimulating hormone concentration 1·4 IU/L (normal 1·4–18·1), and luteinising hormone concentration below 0·07 mIU/L (normal 1·5–9·3). Plasma cortisol concentration was 125 nmol/L (normal >140), and adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was 31·7 ng/L (10·3–48·3). Free T4 concentration was low at 4·98 ng/L (normal 7·0-14·8), with thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1·36 mIU/L (0·35–4·94). A 24-h water balance test showed marked polyuria and polydipsia: with a recorded water intake 5 500 mL and a urine output of 4 000 mL. The plasma osmolality was raised at 294 mOsm/L and the urinary osmolality was low at 246 mOsmol/L; the haematocrit was 51·1%.
A T1-weighted with gadolinium contrast MRI of the hypophysis showed a 6 mm thickening of the pituitary stalk at the optic chiasm level; T2-weighted MRI showed a bulging and plump appearance of the gland (figure). An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan of the brain showed hypermetabolic activity in the pituitary region (figure). A chest CT scan showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with associated pulmonary micronodules. Analysis of fluid obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage indicated lymphocytic alveolitis. Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of a superficial lymph node showed epithelioid cell granulomatous lymphadenitis without necrosis. All microbiological cultures were negative.
Considering the findings in the round: androgen deficiency; adrenal insufficiency; central hypothyroidism—likely responsible for the Raynaud's phenomenon; and diabetes insipidus—indicated by the elevated plasma osmolality with haemoconcentration, which excluded potomania, corroborated by the low urinary osmolality, we diagnosed sarcoidosis involving both the pituitary gland and stalk. The patient was initiated on intramuscular testosterone (250 mg every 3 weeks), hydrocortisone (20 mg daily with an emergency dose of injectable 100 mg), thyroxine 75 μg per day, combined with infliximab, the intravenously administered anti-TNF antibody.
At 6-month follow-up, the patient's overall clinical condition had improved. However, laboratory investigations indicated significant persistent endocrine insufficiency—central hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and androgen insufficiency still requiring replacement therapy. Furthermore, attempts to extend intervals between desmopressin doses led to recurrence of polyuria and polydipsia: indicating ongoing anterior and posterior pituitary insufficiency. A repeat MRI showed that the pituitary stalk had reduced to a maximum thickness of 1 mm, the anterior pituitary flattened against the sella floor, and arachnoidocele; the posterior pituitary maintained a normal hyperintensity and morphology, as seen originally when the patient presented.
Sarcoidosis is a chronic infiltrative and inflammatory condition that may involve any organ, with predilection for the lungs and lymph nodes. Pituitary gland involvement, though less common, has long been recognised by physicians and should be considered. Additionally, it is important to note that endocrine insufficiency is, in most cases, unresponsive to anti-inflammatory treatments—as occurred in our patient.
Differential diagnoses for infiltrative or inflammatory processes affecting the pituitary gland include primary—craniopharyngiomas—and secondary tumours, infections including tuberculosis, IgG-4-related disease, in children Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis, autoimmune hypophysitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sheehan syndrome, and conditions of iron overload.

input: A 27-year-old man was admitted to Shinshu University hospital with overt jaundice and ascites 8 days after long exposure to sunlight. He had been diagnosed with erythropoietic protoporphyria 6 years previously and was prescribed cimetidine (800 mg/day) at that time to downregulate Δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase-2 activity and reduce free protoporphyrin concentrations. Lactulose was also given to promote defaecation and to limit re-absorption of protoporphyrin, although its role in the management of erythropoietic protoporphyria has not been established. The patient was observed to have hallucinations, prolonged prothrombin time (international normalised ratio of 2·1), and elevation of serum total bilirubin (9·5 mg/dL) after admission; as a result, we diagnosed acute liver failure and did two rounds of plasma exchange. Acute viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out by blood tests. His plasma looked icteric under regular white light, but turned red under ultraviolet A in the intensive care unit, suggestive of very high concentrations of porphyrins (figure, A). Ascites drained from the patient also turned red under ultraviolet A (figure, B). Erythrocyte protoporphyrin was markedly increased at the time of admission (5727 μg/dL red blood cells; compared with the normal range of 30–86 μg/dL red blood cells), which supported the diagnosis of rapid aggravation of erythropoietic protoporphyria. After two rounds of plasma exchange, the patient's hepatic function slowly recovered.Hepatopathy induced by erythropoietic protoporphyria can show fulminant aggravation. Since plasma protoporphyrin is very sensitive to light and rapidly declines during sample preparation, erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement is recommended to detect erythropoietic protoporphyria activity. However, this measurement is uncommon and takes time to assess, which can delay accurate diagnosis. Ultraviolet A has increasingly been used in hospitals to check the quality of handwashing. When we encounter patients with acute liver failure of unknown cause, direct examination of body fluids—eg, plasma and ascites—under ultraviolet A could be a simple and useful method to screen for erythropoietic protoporphyria. Samples should therefore be protected from light when a porphyrin measurement is ordered.
options: Acute hepatitis A, Adult-onset type 2 citrullinaemia, Erythropoietic protoporphyria, Wilson’s disease

input:
A 44-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with diabetes at age 21 years presented with a three-day history of oligoarthritis involving both knees and wrists, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the affected joints. Pelvic examination showed a blind-ending vaginal pouch without the cervix. Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1·15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19·3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. Although hypomagnesaemia is a recognised feature of HNF1B-related disease, the association between HNF1B-related disease and CPPD remains uncommon.
This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. HNF1B encodes a transcription factor that is crucial for pancreatic and genitourinary development and plays a key role in magnesium homoeostasis through the regulation of basolateral magnesium transport in the distal convoluted tubule. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and Müllerian anomalies (associated with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss—potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

input: A 53-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of an itchy rash, Raynaud’s phenomenon, dysphagia, and a burning sensation in his hands. Physical examination was notable for firm, greasy papules across his forehead that led to the formation of glabellar grooves (left). There were waxy papules on his hands, with associated skin thickening and finger flexion contractures (right). Similar skin changes were seen on his nose, lips, ears, trunk, and feet. There was no telangiectasia or calcinosis. Sensory neuropathy was present in his hands, arms, and face. Tests of thyroid function were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identified an IgG-monoclonal gammopathy, and a bone marrow biopsy was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options:
1. Light chain (AL) amyloidosis
2. Multiple myeloma
3. Scleredema
4. Scleromyxedema
5. Systemic sclerosis

input:
An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. Oxygen saturation was 96% on room air.
Laboratory investigations showed normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein concentration. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with first-degree heart block. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function with possible bi-leaflet mitral valve prolapse resulting in severe mitral regurgitation (appendix). Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) showed a central jet of mitral regurgitation caused by annular dilatation and non-coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets (figure); using both the standard method—defined as the left ventricular stroke volume minus the aortic net flow—and four-dimensional (4D) flow advanced techniques, the mitral regurgitation was found to be 5 mL (<30 mL is mild; appendix). Additionally, the mitral regurgitation jet was seen swirling around the left atrium, thus leading to an overestimation of the regurgitation using a speckle-doppler trace (figure; video). Furthermore, moderate left ventricular systolic impairment, with a non-ischaemic fibrosis pattern in the lateral and anterior walls, was seen; on T1 mapping, there was globally increased T1 signal and raised extracellular volume (figure). Taken together, the findings suggested non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to cardiac sarcoidosis—and on discussion with the respiratory team, it became apparent that the patient had, 20 years earlier, indeed been treated abroad for sarcoidosis of the lung.
We consequently decided to defer the planned mitral valve surgery, as it was evident—with the information gleaned from the CMR—that the patient had a primary cardiomyopathy and that his symptoms were unrelated to the mild mitral regurgitation. A respiratory review concluded the problem was chronic and recommended close monitoring of the disease.
Multiparametric CMR imaging is invaluable not only for the accurate assessment of function and sub-phenotyping the aetiology of cardiomyopathy, but also, using 4D flow methods, for more precise quantification of mitral regurgitation that might—as shown in our case—completely change the course of clinical management.

output: Mild mitral regurgitation and non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy

input: A 42-year-old woman receiving induction chemotherapy for acute monocytic leukemia developed edematous, erythematous plaques on her face. Biopsy showed perieccrine neutrophilic infiltration with eccrine duct necrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options:

input:
A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol abuse was admitted to our hospital with chronic diarrhoea, confusion, and weakness in both legs. Initial physical examination showed marked cachexia and decreased strength in both lower limbs. His sensation was intact. Laboratory testing showed several electrolyte abnormalities—presumed to be due to his diarrhoea—including hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L); this was gradually corrected over the course of 4 days, using 0·9% sodium chloride. At the end of this period, the sodium was 140 mmol/L (normal range 135–145 mmol/L). Over the next few days, he continued to be encephalopathic and eventually lost motor function of his arms and legs; his pupils continued to be reactive to light and the function of his extraocular muscles remained intact. An MRI scan of his brain showed restricted diffusion and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) showed a corresponding abnormality in the central pons that was consistent with a diagnosis of central pontine demyelination (figure). Sadly, the patient died in the intensive care unit after his family decided to pursue palliative care.
Osmotic demyelination syndrome—also known as central pontine myelinolysis or extrapontine myelinolysis—usually occurs after rapid correction of sodium abnormalities, although it might be seen secondary to chronic alcohol use, other severe electrolyte disturbances, and malnutrition. According to one theory, the lack of sufficient energy in malnourished patients leads to suboptimal functioning of the Na+/K+ATPase pump, which subsequently results in imbalances in sodium homoeostasis in the brain. A high degree of clinical suspicion that it is likely to occur in patients with chronic alcohol use and those who are malnourished might help to prevent the development of osmotic demyelination syndrome. Treatment is usually just supportive management. However, there have been some case reports of successful treatment with plasma exchange, methylprednisone, and immunoglobulins. MRI usually confirms the diagnosis, and the FLAIR sequence is used to suppress the effects of cerebrospinal fluid on the image—this is especially helpful in showing subtle changes at the periphery of the cerebral hemispheres and in the periventricular region.
options: Multiple sclerosis, Schizophrenia, Leptomeningeal disease, Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis

input:
A 45-year-old man with a 5-year history of episodes of smelling a strange odour followed by seeing images of scenes from his childhood, attended our psychiatry department. The patient said that after experiencing the smell and the images, he felt shivery, had piloerection, and was short of breath; each episode lasted about 1 min, with no impairment of consciousness or abnormal movements. The problem tended to occur when he was tired, or sleep deprived. Previously, the episodes occurred once every 3 months, but recently—as his work had become more demanding—they happened more frequently; in the previous month, prior to presenting, they had occurred weekly. The patient reported no accompanying headache and had no history of medical or psychiatric illness.On examination he was generally fit and well; a neurological examination showed no abnormalities; he was left-handed.
Laboratory investigations—including a complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, serum electrolytes, and thyroid function tests—were within normal limits.
MRI of the patient's brain showed a hypointense lesion in the right posterior parahippocampal gyrus on T2 star-weighted imaging, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted imaging, and apparent diffusion coefficient (figure). Hippocampal signal abnormalities were not detected on T1-weighted and T2-weighted imaging. Magnetic resonance angiography showed no abnormalities.
The MRI finding indicated an old intracerebral haemorrhage—insufficient to explain the patient's primary complaints. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed generalised 5 Hz spike and sharp wave complexes with an electrographic maximum in the right anterior temporal scalp electrodes, predominantly in the right hemisphere (appendix). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) with focal seizures secondary to the old intracerebral haemorrhage in the right posterior parahippocampal gyrus. Two weeks after starting carbamazepine, the patient's symptoms had fully resolved.
The differential diagnosis of hallucinations in any modality is extensive. Epilepsy is polymorphic and may mimic a multitude of disorders. An abnormal EEG is most helpful to determine the likely epilepsy type—focal or generalised. TLE is the most common form of localisation-related epilepsy, most frequently appearing in adolescence; hippocampal sclerosis is the most common cause—although it may be caused by structural lesions such as intracerebral haemorrhage or stroke occurring after middle age. Symptoms of focal temporal seizures are characterised by déjà vu, hallucinations, emotional symptoms, epigastric sensations, autonomic features, impairment of awareness or consciousness, and motor manifestations. Olfactory hallucinations are caused by lesions in medial temporal lobe structures—including the anterior parahippocampal gyrus; visual hallucinations occur with right temporal lobe seizures. The right anterior hippocampus relates to topographical hallucinations and the right parahippocampal place area relates to topographical hallucinations along with déjà vu. The semiology of epileptic seizures—as in our case—indicates activation, or dysfunction, of the areas of brain affected.
options: Paranoid schizophrenia, Temporal lobe epilepsy, Delirium, Lewy body disease

A 46-year old nulliparous woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of increasing abdominal pain and pelvic pressure symptoms—including urinary frequency and overflow incontinence of faeces and dyspareunia.4 years earlier, the patient had a laparoscopic myomectomy for multiple uterine myomas: the largest myoma had only been partially excised because of its size and location (6 cm × 7 cm and abutting the rectosigmoid). It was, therefore, shredded using power morcellation—without a containment bag—into smaller pieces which were then retrieved through the laparoscopic port.
On clinical examination we found the patient to have an enlarged uterus of 20 weeks gestational size that was displaced anterosuperior by a significant pelvic mass. MRI on admission showed new uterine and extra-uterine myomas occupying the pelvis (figure). Additionally, some of the myomas were retroperitoneal, and engulfed both major vessels and bowel; these were not present at the original surgery. Following a multidisciplinary team discussion, we decided upon surgical excision to exclude possible malignancy.
En-bloc resection of the recto-sigmoid and pelvic side wall myomas, total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (figure), omental biopsy, and end-colostomy (Hartmann's) were performed. Histopathological examination of samples obtained during the operation showed benign myomas—with no evidence of malignancy—and confirmed that they were uterine in origin.
At follow-up 3 months later, MRI showed no signs of residual intrapelvic disease; the patient remains asymptomatic and reports an improved quality of life.
We believe that the source of the retroperitoneal myomas might have been the large fibroid that was only partially excised during the first procedure 4 years earlier; the development of some of the myomas was probably independent of the surgery. However, some of the leiomyomas—both intra-uterine and retroperitoneal—might have been spread as an unintended consequence of the power morcellation being done without a containment bag resulting in seeding of cells sprayed during shredding.
Power morcellation—useful for minimally invasive surgery—has been the subject of much debate due to the risk of disseminating occult malignant tumours. While this has rightly been a focus of informed consent and the development of guidelines, the consequences of morcellation on benign tumours have been less discussed; as illustrated here by our case, although rare, these can lead to serious morbidity, and should therefore, also be discussed in shared decision making and informed consent. Furthermore, it is important to employ meticulous surgical technique and containment morcellation bags to preserve oncological hygiene—a situation frequently overlooked in benign cases (video).
output: it should always be performed with in-bag morcellator
target: it is very commonly associated with visceral damage
options: it is very commonly associated with visceral damage, it should always be performed with in-bag morcellator, it should not be used in postmenopausal women or when there is a suspicion of malignancy because it can upstage an existing cancer, it can decrease length of hospital stay, enhance recovery, and improve cosmetic outcome

input: A 35-year-old Libyan woman was referred to us from another institution with the diagnosis of massive pericardial effusion and pericardial tamponade. On admission to us, she was hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Electrocardiography showed unspecific low QRS voltage and ST-T segment flattening. Chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly. We did an emergency pericardial aspiration which yielded 1500 ml of yellow coloured fluid. A transthoracic echocardiogrm showed multiple cystic formations approximately 1·5–2 cm within the pericardial cavity (figure A), and confirmed the need for surgery. We did a standard median sternotomy and thoroughly irrigated the pericardium with hypertonic saline; multiple cysts were removed from the pericardium (figures B and C). Our patient was diagnosed with a ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst and pericardial tamponade. We established the diagnosis based on the gross appearance of the removed cysts, the echocardiogram results, and a high ESR. Hydatid disease is endemic in Libya, a southern Mediterranean country. Serological tests were not available. After surgery she was treated with oral albendazole for 12 days. She recovered well and was discharged 12 days after surgery. Pericardial tamponade due to hydatid disease is a rare condition that has been seldom reported in the literature.
options: Augmentin, Albendazole, Fluconazole, Dexmethasone

input:
A 50-year old man who had not travelled outside the UK for the past 20 years—but who had lived in Angola for most of his childhood—presented at our clinic with a 4-week history of worsening exercise tolerance. The patient had undergone renal transplantation 2 years and 6 years previously. Since transplantation, his estimated glomerular filtration rate had been slowly decreasing, most likely due to chronic graft rejection, and he was therefore on high-dose immunosuppression treatment with tacrolimus 8 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and prednisolone 5 mg once daily. On physical examination, he was afebrile but had a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per min. No crepitations were heard in his chest on auscultation and there was no evidence of fluid overload. An arterial blood gas analysis showed a partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 134 mm Hg on 8 L of oxygen. On admission, blood tests showed a haemoglobin concentration of 10·6 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 3·7 × 109 per L, with a neutrophil cell count of 29 × 109 per L, a lymphocyte cell count of 0·2 × 109 per L, and an eosinophil count of 0·1 × 109 per L. Chest x-ray and subsequent chest CT showed reticulonodular shadowing throughout both lung fields. Sputum PCR was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii and treatment for pneumonia—including an increase in the dose of prednisolone to 40 mg twice a day—was started.Strongyloides stercoralis serology was requested and was found to be negative. The patient's health deteriorated on the fifth day of his admission: his PaO2 was 67 mm Hg on air and he required ventilatory support. A bronchoalveolar lavage was done and microscopy of the resulting fluid showed filariform larvae of S stercoralis (figure). A diagnosis of strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome (SHS) was therefore made. However, despite several more days of treatment with ivermectin 200 μg/kg per day (13 mg) via a nasogastric tube, the patient died.
SHS is a life-threatening condition that usually affects immunosuppressed individuals. It can present over 30 years after initial infection. Serology can be falsely negative in SHS and eosinophilia is often not seen. Screening of potential donors and recipients of transplants from areas endemic for strongyloidiasis—including Africa, Asia, and Latin America—and subsequent pre-emptive treatment with ivermectin should be considered in all patients at high risk.
options: Aspergillosis, Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, CMV pneumonitis, Strongyloidiasis stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome

input: A 28-year-old woman came to our clinic saying she had blurred vision in her right eye. 22 h earlier, she had noticed areas of darkness in the lower half of her right visual field. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50 000 outpatients. The causes of retinal arterial occlusion in young adults—different from those in older individuals—include systemic vasculitis, migraine, sickle-cell haemoglobinopathy, myeloproliferative disorders, hypercoagulable states, use of oral contraceptives, and intravenous drug abuse. Valvular heart disease—originating from rheumatic fever—remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.
image_path: ./data/images/lancet_images/Keeping an eye out for systemic disease.jpg
options: Cataract, Retinal artery occlusion, Uveitis, Conjunctivitis

input:
A 50-year-old man attended our specialised clinic reporting swelling, paraesthesia, discolouration, and fatigue in both arms while doing physical activity. The patient said the problem was particularly bad when lifting objects above his shoulders; his right side was worse than his left.Notably in his medical history, the patient, aged 32 years, was diagnosed with deep venous thrombosis in his left arm which developed after a period of strenuous physical activity; lifelong anticoagulant treatment was initiated at that time and he was switched to apixaban 3 months before we saw him. Also, aged 46 years, he had a further thrombosis in his right subclavian vein; it was successfully treated with thrombolysis followed by 2 years of fenprocoumon. Thrombophilia screening was negative, and a CT scan found no predisposing factors for thrombosis and no skeletal anomalies—including cervical ribs or anomalies of the clavicular bones. Additionally, no soft tissue abnormalities were identified. After the second episode, the treating physicians felt that both thromboses were primary—or spontaneous—since no trauma had been involved and the first episode had developed after vigorous activity.
Examination of the patient at our specialist centre found him to be fit and healthy looking; his heart rate was 81 beats per min and regular, and his blood pressure was 127/72 mm Hg. A cardiovascular examination found no murmurs or gallops and intact radial and ulnar pulses. Neurological examination was normal; we found no swelling, skin discolouration, or other evidence of venous obstruction at rest. The Eden test—or military brace test—provoked his complaints and both cephalic veins became distended.
An x-ray of the thoracic aperture showed no cervical ribs or bony anomalies of the first rib; venography in four positions showed no abnormalities at the costoclavicular junctions in the neutral position, abduction, or adduction. In a military attitude position, significant effacement of the veins was seen at the site of the pectoralis minor on both sides—indicating thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS; figure).
A 2-stage trans-axillary pectoral minor tenectomy was done and the patient immediately reported relief of his symptoms. Postoperative venography showed no further compression (appendix) and the anticoagulation was stopped. 1 year after surgery, the patient was asymptomatic—even during strenuous activities.
TOS disorders result from compression of either nerves, veins, or arteries in the thoracic outlet. Venous TOS is caused by repetitive extrinsic compression and resultant injury to the subclavian vein at the bony thoracic outlet. Symptoms in the arms are caused by intermittent positional obstruction without thrombosis—known as McCleery syndrome—or with acute or chronic thrombosis—known as effort thrombosis or Paget-von Schröetter syndrome. Compression of the subclavian vein usually occurs at the junction of the first rib and the clavicle: costoclavicular junction. Obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle at the retropectoralis space—as seen in our patient—is relatively rare.
Patients with positional intermittent subclavian vein obstruction will present with episodic arm discolouration and swelling, usually elicited by either exercise or arm elevation; venograms can be normal at rest. Investigation using venography—rather than CT or MRI—we believe, is preferable since it facilitates communication between the radiologist and patient making it easier to elicit symptoms, and at the same time, observing the compression. If dynamic positioning shows no compression at the costoclavicular junction, the possibility of obstruction by the pectoralis minor muscle must be considered (video).
options: Venous thoracic outlet syndrome, Thrombophilia, Systemic vasculitis, Malignancy

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20·0 g/dL; normal 13·2–16·6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38–48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8–25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12–16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20·1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1–3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet—symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients—like ours—whose PDAs are inoperable (video).
image_path: ./data/images/lancet_images/Clubbing of the toes and sparing the fingers with a patent ductus arteriosus and reversed shunting.jpg
options: sildenafil, bosentan, ambrisentan, verapamil

input:
A 50-year-old man with a 2-year history of a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea was referred to our lung disease clinic. The patient—who was originally from Turkey—had a significant cigarette smoking history but no relevant occupational exposures.Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest x-ray was normal and lung function testing showed a moderate reduction in diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide: 72% predicted. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest demonstrated extensive septal thickening and ground glass abnormalities in a crazy-paving pattern (figure; appendix).
Differential diagnoses we considered at this stage included organising pneumonia, lymphangitic spread of a tumour, lipoid pneumonia, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and atypical infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii.
A bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsies were performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was normal in appearance and no pathogens were identified. Transbronchial biopsy showed architecturally preserved alveoli filled with amorphous material positive for periodic acid-Schiff, granular material, and foamy alveolar macrophages (figure).
Immunohistochemistry showed surfactant protein B proprotein in the intra-alveolar material and cytoplasmic staining in the adjacent alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes (appendix). Surfactant protein C proprotein was also expressed in alveolar epithelial type II pneumocytes but absent in the intra-alveolar material (appendix).
Taken together, the findings were consistent with a diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) syndrome. Serum concentration of antibodies to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) was raised at 33 μg/mL (normal <5), confirming the diagnosis. Over the subsequent 12 months, the patient reported increasing dyspnoea on exertion and his pulmonary function tests declined. He is under consideration for whole lung lavage or inhaled recombinant GM-CSF therapy.
PAP is a rare syndrome characterised by alveolar surfactant accumulation resulting in progressive dyspnoea and hypoxaemic respiratory failure. Autoimmune PAP accounts for 90–95% of cases; notably dust exposure, infection, and myelodysplastic syndrome are among several secondary causes of PAP.
An important clinical feature of PAP is a discrepancy between the severity of chest CT findings and patients' symptoms—as seen in our patient whose symptoms were mild despite a markedly abnormal chest CT. GM-CSF autoantibody levels in serum are reported to be close to 100% sensitive and specific for autoimmune PAP, and their measurement can prevent delay in the diagnosis. Surgical lung biopsy and transbronchial lung biopsy are often non-diagnostic due to the patchy distribution of the disease and are associated with potential morbidity; additionally, they do not provide further understanding of the underlying cause of PAP. Identifying the cause of PAP is important as new, targeted therapies—including aerosolised GM-CSF in autoimmune PAP—are emerging for this rare but underdiagnosed condition (video).
image_path: ./data/images/lancet_images/A discrepancy between CT findings and clinical presentation.jpg
options: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis

input: In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per μL). White blood cell count and concentrations of creatine kinase were normal (52 units per L; reference range: 34–171 units per L). Nasopharyngeal exudate was negative for influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). A chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Symptomatic treatment with oral analgesics and antipyretics (paracetamol 650 mg every 8 h, alternating every 4 h with dipyrone 575 mg every 8 h) was initiated, and the patient showed clinical improvement 4 days after admission. The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient did not seek medical attention and was not evaluated by a physician until the 3-week follow-up. During this follow-up, the patient reported the fever and headache recurrence, and analysis indicated increased concentrations of inflammatory markers (14 mg/dL of C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm per h). The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A subsequent visceral arteriography showed multiple microaneurysms in the small arteries of the digestive visceral territory and both renal arteries, which suggested polyarteritis nodosa vasculitis (figure). Tests for antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV serological tests were negative. There was no evidence to suggest the involvement of other organs (five factor score=0). The patient received treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone bolus for 2 days (120 mg daily). The patient was discharged and received oral azathioprine (100 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 150 mg daily indefinitely) and a tapering regimen of oral prednisone (30 mg daily for 1 week, followed by 20 mg daily for 1 week, 1 week off, 10 mg daily for 2 weeks, alternate daily doses of 10 mg and 7·5 mg for 2 weeks, and 7·5 mg daily indefinitely). At the 3-week follow-up, fever, headache, and myalgia had resolved.Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare necrotising vasculitis of medium and small arteries, with substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Clinical features are highly variable; symptoms at onset are usually unspecific, and the differential diagnosis is often broad. Because the patient was admitted during the COVID-19 pandemic, the possibility of an infection with SARS-CoV-2 was initially considered; however, the poor clinical and analytical improvement prompted us to look for other causes of the symptoms and laboratory abnormalities. Accurate diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa allowed for early initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.

options: Mycotic aneurysms of the visceral arteries in endocarditis, Microaneurysms in polyarteritis nodosa, Stenosis of the visceral arteries in thromboangiitis obliterans, Thrombosis of the visceral arteries in COVID-19

input:
An 18-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital for investigation of repeated episodes of rectal bleeding. Over the preceding 5 months the patient had made 4 visits to our emergency room reporting bleeding from the rectum. The problem was not associated with any other symptoms and was self-limiting. Previously, fresh red blood had been found on digital rectal examination, with no other abnormalities; no haemorrhoids, fistulous tracts, or abscesses had been found, and the patient had normal tone of her anal sphincter.Laboratory tests found a typical haemoglobin concentration (14·6 g/dL) with no iron deficiency (82 μg/dL), and a normal ferritin concentration (87 ng/mL).
We carried out an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, to investigate possible causes of the patient's low vitamin B12, which showed no abnormalities. However, at colonoscopy—40 cm from the anal margin at the junction between the sigmoid colon and rectum—we found a large lesion with vascular malformations. Further examination was not possible because, we considered, the risk of bleeding was too high. Therefore, to accurately categorise the lesion, we did a CT angiogram, which showed a vascular abnormality in the wall of the sigmoid colon with vascular ectasia and phleboliths—indicative of a haemangioma-type lesion that would account for the patient's repeated, self-limiting history of bleeding (figure).
Following discussion with the patient about the pros and cons of surgery, we carried out a laparoscopic investigation which showed a large vascular lesion extending from the middle to the proximal part of the sigmoid colon. We proceeded to open surgical resection of the mass and completing a lateral terminal colorectal anastomosis. Notably during the operation, we found the haemangioma was 10·0 cm × 7·0 cm × 20·5 cm; the serosa was dilated, and multiple raised white congestive protuberances were seen.
Histopathological examination of a sample of a biopsy of the excised lesion confirmed it to be a cavernous haemangioma—present in the submucosa, muscularis propria, and subserous fat. No signs of malignancy were observed.
Haemangiomas are classified as capillary, cavernous, arteriovenous, venous, intramuscular, and synovial. They usually occur on the skin in infants but may infrequently develop in internal organs including the liver, brain, and—as in our patient—in the gut; approximately 80% of colonic haemangiomas are cavernous in type and capillary account for less than 10% of cases. Cavernous haemangiomas are most frequently accompanied by bleeding and anaemia. Rarely, they may cause obstruction, intussusception, and platelet sequestration.
Rectal bleeding may be caused by a wide range of pathologies including colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, haemorrhoids, and anal fissures. Rectal bleeding as a solitary symptom has a positive predictive value for colon cancer of 8% in patients aged over 50 years. Age may be a valuable clue in deciding upon the diagnosis, but it would be wise not to dismiss the possibility of colorectal malignancy in a young person.
options: Lymphoma, Haemangioma, Multiple polyps, Diverticulitis

A 72-year-old man was seen in our department for a treadmill electrocardiogram (ECG) stress test; he had previously been diagnosed with stable angina and was on maximum anti-ischaemia treatment—including nifedipine, atenolol, transdermal nitroglycerin, and ranolazine. The patient had a history of 3-vessel coronary artery surgical revascularisation, which had been done 26 years before.After 5 minutes of exercise, significant ST-segment depression was seen in leads V2 to V6 of the 12-lead ECG—although the patient did not report any angina—and the test was stopped. The ECG abnormalities persisted in the recovery period, and, by way of a comparison, we asked the patient to record his own precordial ECG with his smartwatch. He made the recording by placing the back of his Apple Watch near the V5 electrode and touching the watch's digital crown with the index finger of his right hand. The standard 12-lead ECG showed persistent ST depression (figure) and three monomorphic premature ventricular complexes. A final premature ventricular complex fell on the preceding T wave—R on T—and triggered ventricular fibrillation which resulted in the patient losing consciousness; he was effectively resuscitated with a defibrillator. Since a conventional 12-lead ECG was being recorded simultaneously when the arrhythmia started, we could verify the similarity of the V5 lead ECG with the record made with the patient's smartwatch (figure). The Apple Watch also correctly recorded the ST depression, the premature ventricular complexes, and the episode of ventricular fibrillation.
After a coronary angiography showed non-revascularisable coronary artery disease, the patient was fitted with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; he was allowed home 6 days later. At this stage the dose of the β blocker was increased to the maximum tolerated dose.
Smartwatches can monitor a wide range of normal and abnormal physiology—including heart rate, blood oxygen, and ECG rhythms. Portable monitoring devices are mainly intended to diagnosis of atrial fibrillation; however—as our case shows—they can also accurately record ST depression, premature ventricular complexes, and ventricular fibrillation.
options: Atrioventricular block, Ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, Inducible ischaemia, Ectopic premature ventricular beats

input: A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of a pustular rash on both hands. A 69-year-old woman with a history of myocardial infarction came to hospital after more than 24 h of intermittent chest pain, shortness of breath, and diaphoresis. On admission, a 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischaemia. Biomarkers of myocardial necrosis were negative. A portable chest radiograph and a bedside transthoracic echocardiogram showed pathognomonic findings of acute type A aortic dissection (figure; videos). The patient underwent urgent repair of the aortic root. The patient survived the immediate postoperative course despite complications of haemodynamic instability, hypotension, and acute renal failure, but later succumbed to multiorgan failure.
Delayed presentation of acute aortic syndrome is plagued by high mortality and morbidity. The location of the intimal tear in acute type A aortic dissection is in the immediate vicinity of the sinuses of Valsalva 65% of the time. The sensitivity and specificity of chest radiography is 81% and 89%, respectively. The sensitivity of transthoracic echocardiography is between 78% and 100%; its specificity ranges from 87% to 96%. Transthoracic echocardiography is a valuable diagnostic tool in cases when more sensitive techniques (transoesophageal echocardiography, CT, magnetic resonance angiography) are not readily available or are impractical.
options: Intravenous esmolol, Intravenous sodium nitroprusside, Systemic thrombolytic therapy, Surgical therapy

A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm—between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38·9°C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze—known as the sun-setting sign—and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12×109per μ per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery—the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention—including drainage if possible, as in our case—followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome—the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

options: Hydrocephalus, Focal motor deficient, Visual impairment, Epilepsy

A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall—known as a scaphoid abdomen—was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9·9 g/dL (normal range 9·5–14); serum sodium concentration was 138·5 mmol/L (normal range 136·0–145·0) and potassium concentration was 3·7 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries—as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.
Road traffic crashes are the leading cause of death of children and young adults aged 5–29 years with an estimated 1·19 million deaths each year, according to a recent WHO report. About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4–5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda—according to WHO—ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100 000 people compared to 24·1 deaths per 100 000 in the African region and globally to 18·1 deaths per 100 000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19·4% (4806 deaths of 24 728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians—as in our patient—constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor—further cerebellar signs—were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment—he had completed 11 years of full-time education—but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder—a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. When a premutation occurs—with between 55 and 200 CGG repeats—the FMR1 gene expresses high levels of mRNA, which results in toxicity and consequently the neurodegenerative condition of FXTAS. Management involves symptomatic therapy: medications, psychological counselling, and rehabilitative treatments. Genetic counselling should be given to all individuals with FXTAS and family members.
output: All daughters of men with FXTAS are obligate FMRI premutation carriers
target: Daughters of men with FXTAS have a 50% chance of having the syndrome
options: All sons of men with FXTAS will have fragile X syndrome, All daughters of men with FXTAS are obligate FMRI premutation carriers, Daughters of men with FXTAS have a 50% chance of having the syndrome, Women with FXTAS have a 50% chance of having a child with the mutation

input: Various cases in professional sports have brought the matter of doping—the use of performance-enhancing drugs—to the attention of the broad public. Here, we present a case of doping in a 21-year-old amateur bodybuilder. The man presented to our clinic feeling generally unwell. He was subfebrile and had massive, deep ulcerations, abscesses, and pustules located on his chest and upper back (figure). Persistent questioning revealed a history of continuous abuse of anabolic-androgenic steroids (testosterone enantate 250 mg plus metandienona 30 mg twice weekly), which was consistent with the diagnosis of a severe acne conglobata that was anabolic-androgenic steroid induced. Additional investigations showed a substantial impairment in sperm concentration and reduced testicular volume. Skin lesions showed rapid improvement after discontinuation of anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse and with antiseptic and antibiotic therapy. However, the extensive scarring is likely to remain with the young man for the rest of his life.
options: Pyoderma gangrenosum, Necrotising fasciitis, Acne conglobata, Dermatitis herpetiformis

input: A 46-year-old woman, with no contributory history, presented with a 7 month growth in her right hallux. Initially, she had noticed a dark discolouration of the distal aspect of the toe, followed by a gradual non-tender swelling and subsequent effacement of the nail (figure). Results of an initial biopsy suggested that it could be a brown tumour, which prompted further biochemical tests, the results of which revealed a parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 154 ng/L and a serum calcium concentration of 2·67 mmol/L in the setting of normal renal function and vitamin D sufficiency. Her 24 h urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio did not fit the criteria for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Results of parathyroid scintigraphy showed a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan of the distal radius revealed a bone mineral density of 0·471 g/cm2 (T score −3·7; Z score −3·1). After a right inferior parathyroidectomy and a disarticulation of the distal hallux, PTH fell to 23 ng/L and serum calcium to 2·0 mmol/L. Pathology confirmed the presence of a parathyroid adenoma and a brown tumour of the hallux.
options: Hyperthyroidism, Hypothyroidism, Hyperparathyroidism, Hypoparathyroidism

input:
A 31-year-old man with Wilson's disease presented with a pruritic rash across the neck of 12 months' duration. His disease had been well controlled on penicillamine (500 mg twice daily) with pyridoxine (25 mg daily) for many years. There had been no new medications, trauma, animal contact, or change in detergents, clothing, or environment before rash onset. Physical examination revealed two annular lesions on the ventral and posterior neck, which were well demarcated with serpiginous, raised borders and central clearing (figure, A and B). There were no other lesions present. Full blood count, liver function tests, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits aside from a chronically increased alkaline phosphatase concentration (179 U/L, reference range 40–130 U/L). Coeliac serology was negative. The rash had not resolved with previous empirical courses of systemic and topical antifungal medication for presumed dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis). A 2-mm punch biopsy of the rash was done and the histology results are shown (figure, C and D).Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a rare complication of penicillamine therapy for Wilson's disease and might also be seen in association with systemic diseases such as Ehlers Danlos and Down's syndrome. It is a chronic dermatosis characterised by extrusion of elastic fibre aggregates through the epidermis. The exact mechanism of pencillamine-related elastosis perforans serpiginosa is unclear, but has been postulated to occur indirectly as a result of impairment of lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, which has an important role in dermal elastic fibre cross-linking, as well as directly through formation of complexes with elastic fibre precursors, leading to impaired elastic fibre maturation. The diagnosis is made clinically and histologically with the characteristic findings illustrated in the figures.
As seen in our case, this chronic dermatosis is often seen in the second decade of life, following prolonged use of penicillamine. The rash distribution is variable, involving the neck and upper limbs most commonly. Although regression is possible with cessation of penicillamine, scarring and atrophy could persist indefinitely. Misdiagnosis is common and continued use of penicillamine risks progression of rash and permanent scarring. In this case, penicillamine was changed to trientene as an alternative chelating agent to manage the Wilson's disease. Despite its similar mechanism of action to penicillamine, there have been no published case reports of trientene-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa to our knowledge. 4 weeks after cessation of penicillamine, the rash persisted unchanged.
options: Tinea Corporis, Elastosis Perforans Serpiginosa, Perforating Granuloma Annulare, Dermatitis Herpetiformis

input:
A 37-year-old man living in northwest Ohio, USA, presented with a cough, haemoptysis, and weight loss, all observed for 2 months. The patient emigrated from Taiwan at the age of 3 years and now works in a parcel warehouse. He had no history of incarceration or travel outside of the USA.Chest x-ray and contrast-enhanced CT (appendix) showed a left upper lobe lesion with associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A transbronchial biopsy with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures was negative, and histopathology showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation. A four-drug regimen (daily standard weight-based dosing of rifampicin [600 mg], isoniazid [300 mg], ethambutol [1600 mg], and pyrazinamide [2000 mg]) was started for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.
After completing 6 months of therapy for tuberculosis, the patient was readmitted to hospital, this time complaining of multiple tender, cutaneous lesions on his face, torso, and extremities; some were verrucous and others nodular (figure). He also had headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Haemogram results showed a white blood cell count of 22 000 cells per μL with 91% segmented neutrophils. An ELISA test for HIV was negative. The chest CT revealed near complete resolution of the lung lesion; however, a CT of the head and neck (appendix) showed numerous white matter ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally in the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, and cerebellar hemispheres, as well as a retropharyngeal abscess.
Subcutaneous nodules were drained and histopathology showed broad-based, thick-walled budding yeast suggestive of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Urine antigen testing for B dermatitidis was positive, and fungal cultures from surgical specimens grew B dermatitidis after 1 week.
4 weeks of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day, followed by 12 months of oral voriconazole (300 mg twice daily), led to resolution of skin and brain lesions. Voriconazole has become one of the preferred options for oral stepdown when CNS drug penetration is desired. Disseminated cases of blastomycosis should include CNS imaging even in the absence of CNS-related symptoms. Diagnosis might require multiple testing modalities for improved sensitivity.
options: Acute angle branching septated hyphae, Broad-based budding yeasts, Granulomatous inflammation with positive acid fast staining, Beaded branching Gram-positive rod organisms, weakly positive on AFB stain

input: A 33-year-old man was referred to our internal medicine department after an ophthalmic examination revealed a bilateral granulomatous anterior and intermediate uveitis with papillitis (figure A) associated with retinal dystrophy features (figure B). The patient had been experiencing decreased vision for several months and had a history of childhood-onset bilateral arthritis, involving proximal and distal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints. His sister, mother, and uncle were previously treated for idiopathic uveitis and papillitis. He reported recurrent headaches and anhidrosis. Physical examination revealed hand deformities (figure C) with nail dystrophy and melanonychia (figure D) and an enlarged spleen (20 cm). X-rays showed erosions of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints (figure E). Laboratory investigations found elevated C-reactive protein (86 mg/L, normal range <5 mg/L), but normal white blood cell counts (normal count, 6.48 g/L). Thorough investigation for infectious diseases and autoimmune biomarkers were negative. Because of the familial context and a recent observation of a similar phenotype, we did targeted sequencing of the ALPK1 gene, which encodes α kinase 1, in the patient and his sister. We found the heterozygous missense variant (p.Thr237Met) in the patient and his sister, which has previously been reported to cause retinal dystrophy, optic nerve oedema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and headache (ROSAH) syndrome. Treatment was started with intravenous tocilizumab at a dose of 8 mg/kg every 4 weeks. ALPK1 is a recently described intracellular pattern-recognition receptor, which senses metabolites of several bacteria. ROSAH syndrome is an autoinflammatory disease with a highly variable phenotype, including (in addition to the ROSAH-defining features) recurrent fever, cytopenias, dental and nail abnormalities, sicca syndrome, and meningeal inflammation on brain MRI. To date, about 60 people have been described as having the syndrome worldwide. The best treatment remains unknown, but biologics targeting tumour necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-1, and IL-6 have shown efficacy in suppressing systemic inflammation. This large spectrum of inflammatory features can mimic Blau syndrome; however, a rash is common in this disease, whereas it has not been described in ROSAH syndrome.Rheumatologists should consider ROSAH syndrome in patients presenting childhood-onset arthritis with X-ray erosive changes and hand deformities in a context of a family history of eye disease.

options: Blau syndrome, ROSAH syndrome, Neuro-Behçet, Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

input:
The skeleton of a human being buried over 1000 years ago, in the medieval archaeological site of Torre Velha, in north-eastern Portugal, was referred to us for analysis and investigation (appendix).On examination, we found the outstandingly well preserved skeleton of an adult who was likely to have been more than 25 years old at the time of death. The person was approximately 1·80 m tall. Notably, out of the six skeletons examined, where height could be ascertained, this individual was the tallest (appendix). Based on pelvic morphology and metric analysis of the skeleton, we concluded that the individual was a man. However, the bi-iliac width of our person was 289 mm, considerably larger than the average width previously reported for ancient Portuguese men (mean 261·8 mm; SD=13·4; Student's t test: t=22·6944; df=124; p<0·001). Additionally, the individual's teeth were worn asymmetrically, indicating probable malocclusion of the jaw and maxillary prognathism (figure; appendix). Bone densitometry analysis showed normal bone mineral density values (0·792–0·999 g/cm2).
Genetic analysis was undertaken using a variety of different methodologies—including the calculation of X chromosome to Y chromosome autosome ratios (0·902 and 0·298, respectively), X chromosome and Y chromosome dosages (approximately 2 and 1, respectively), and X chromosome heterozygosity (approximately 0·2). We also determined the Y chromosome haplogroup to be R1b-P310 (R1b1a1b1a1), a frequent western-European and pan-European lineage, in accordance with the individual's Iberian genetic ancestry (appendix).
Furthermore, using a novel Bayesian method, allowing us to probabilistically assign individuals to karyotypes based on the number of sequencing reads—or DNA fragments sequenced—mapping to the X, Y, or autosomal chromosomes, we concluded our individual's karyotype to be 47,XXY, and rejected models of contamination of XXY and XX or XY (figure; appendix). The closeness of the observed position of the studied individual and theoretical position for an XXY karyotype (figure) strongly agrees with our posterior probability of approximately 1 for this individual having a Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype. Considering the morphological findings—specifically the height, the bi-iliac width, the possible jaw malocclusion, and the maxillary prognathism—the genetic findings—indicating a karyotype of 47,XXY—we concluded that the studied individual had Klinefelter's syndrome.
The prevalence of Klinefelter's syndrome in the general population has previously been reported to be 0·1–0·2%, but many patients remain undiagnosed.
Typically, people with Klinefelter's syndrome are tall, have broad hips, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynaecomastia; they may have mandibular prognathism. Obesity, low glucose tolerance, and diabetes are observed, as well as osteoporosis because of androgen deficiency. Notably, the absence of osteoporosis in our case does not preclude a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome; osteoporosis is only present in approximately 10–40% of cases. Genetically, about 80% of cases are 47,XXY.
DNA from osteological remains is often scarce, degraded, fragmented, and unsuitable for analysis using commonly available techniques for clinical diagnosis of chromosomal aneuploidies. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel Bayesian method, which, we believe, is a potentially efficient statistical way of analysing fragmented DNA from a variety of sources (eg, ancient DNA, cell-free DNA, and DNA from forensic cases).
output: Robust morphology, tall stature, and a probable malocclusion
target: Robust morphology, tall stature, and a probable malocclusion
options: Robust morphology, extremely short stature, and no signs of osteoporosis, Robust morphology, tall stature, and a probable malocclusion, While most physical traits are variable, signs of osteoporosis are always associated with Klinefelter’s syndrome, No physical traits can be observed in the skeleton of an individual with Klinefelter’s syndrome

input: A 72-year-old man visited the surgical outpatient clinic with a spontaneous fracture of his left wrist. Physical examination suggested an additional fracture of his right wrist. Conventional radiograph showed extensive osteolytic lesions with fractures of both distal ulnae (figure). He reported no recent weight loss, night sweats, prostatic problems, or deteriorating performance status. There was no lymphadenopathy on physical examination. Positron emission tomography showed no primary tumour in the abdomen or thorax and no other skeletal lesions, nor was there any suspicion of prostate carcinoma. Microscopic and immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy of the left ulna showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. No malignant cells were seen in bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy. A diagnosis of primary osseous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, stage IIE, was made. Given the striking anatomical features, treatment with three cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) and local radiotherapy was initiated.
options: Skeletal angiomas, Sudeck’s atrophy, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Gorham’s disease
